According to recent reports, a, Datasets were curated and compiled as described in Fig. 1a. The remaining pipeline was run separately and in parallel for mouse and human data. All computation was performed in R. Schematic created in BioRender; Wang, H. https://biorender.com/w8x4pii (2026). b, Quality control metrics included ensuring that the number of unique genes per cell (nFeature_RNA) was > 200 and the fraction of mitochondrial reads was <20%. Cells with nFeature_RNA ≥ 95th percentile were also removed as a precaution against doublets. c, Data were then converted into an optimized read/write disk space using BPCells. d, To further streamline computation, all data were then sketched into representative 1,000-cell subsets on a per-study basis. e, The resulting data (12.8 M cells for human or 2.5 M cells for mouse) were then integrated on a per-study basis using three independent approaches (Harmony, scVI, FastMNN), resulting in three distinct clusterings and uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) embeddings. f, Each of the three objects from e were annotated independently in a semi-supervised fashion using canonical markers in conjunction with the automated classification toolkits SingleR and scATOMIC, resulting in seven coarse cell type designations for each of the three distinct objects. g, For each of the six TME cell types (epithelial cells are excluded moving forward), separate and parallel computational pipelines were followed. This begins with pooling all cells designated as a given cell type (e.g., fibroblasts) by any of the three integration approaches, and creating a common object. h, Each cell type-specific object undergoes re-integration using study-specific batch keys, followed by normalization, scaling, principal component analysis (PCA), UMAP, clustering, and re-annotation to assess purity. Improperly classified cells are then removed, and this process of recursive cleaning is repeated until all cells are found to be of the correct cell type. i, Once all cells are found to be correctly classified, the final atlas for that cell type is annotated and final subpopulations are determined. j, As described above, the process from g to i is repeated→ separately for each of the primary six TME cell types in this atlas.

In a recent development, a, Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) embeddings of 1,000 sketched cells per study integrated using Harmony, scVI, and FastMNN integration techniques. b, UMAP projections of sketched results from each integration approach onto all 12.8 million single cells in the human atlas. Cells are grouped into seven main cell type clusters. c, Dot plots indicating expression levels of characteristic markers for each of the seven cell types. d, Venn diagrams showing overlap in cell annotations among the three integration approaches and the final atlas. e, Ratios of the number of cells in the intersection versus union of Venn diagrams for each cell type in d. Notably, applying the intersection excludes many cells that may be desirable to include in the final atlas. f, Ratio of cells for each type that are included the final atlas compared to those that would have been arrived at by using the intersection of the three integration approaches. Ratios greater than one indicate the presence of cells in our final atlas that would otherwise have been excluded using an intersectional approach. Illustration of the human created in BioRender; Wang, H. https://biorender.com/q41gtvr (2026).

Industry observers note that top-left, UMAP projection based on inferred CNV profiles, where individual cells are colored by their global CNV score. Higher scores (yellow) indicate a greater degree of chromosomal aberration, while lower scores (dark blue) represent cells with profiles closer to the diploid reference. Top-right, The same CNV-based UMAP embedding, with cells colored according to our cell type annotations. The spatial clustering indicates that different cell lineages share similar large-scale genomic gains and losses. Bottom, Heatmap of inferred large-scale CNV patterns. Rows are labeled according to our cell type annotations. Columns represent genomic coordinates, with ticks indicating chromosome boundaries. Color corresponds to relative CNV intensity, where red denotes genomic gains and blue denotes genomic losses. CNV inference was performed on a 100,000-cell subset of the human atlas.

Sources indicate that a–d, Dot plots displaying the expression of characteristic, subpopulation-defining marker genes for fibroblasts (a), endothelial cells (b), mural cells (c), and nerve cells (d). Dot size represents the percentage of cells within a given subpopulation expressing the indicated gene, and color intensity denotes the average scaled expression level. To further validate the lineage specificity of these annotations, the rightmost columns of each plot display the absence of expression for established marker genes corresponding to alternative parent cell types (designated as non-fibroblast, non-endothelial, non-mural, and non-nerve, respectively).

a–d, UMAP embeddings of the human atlas coloured by per-cell SCENIC regulon activity score, showing higher activity of the RUNX3(+) and IKZF1(+) regulons in apCAFs (a), the ETV7(+) and IRF2(+) regulons in ISG15+ iCAFs (b), the CREB3L1(+) and NKX3-2(+) regulons in mCAFs (c), and the CEBPA(+) and FOXO3(+) regulons in ssCAFs (d). e, Analysis of metabolic programs for all stromal populations using scMetabolism. f–h, Metabolic activity for CAFs (f), endothelial cells (g), and mural cells (h). a–h, Analyses were performed on 100,000-cell subsets of the human atlas. e–h, Dot size and colour denote the scMetabolism pathway activity score for each population.

Sources indicate that a, Cells from the Kang et al. cancer stromal atlas were assessed by the latest scTME R package and classified using level 2 (fine) cell typing, showing high concordance among fibroblast and endothelial subpopulations, with differences primarily in fibroblast nomenclature. b, Cells from the Nieto et al. cancer immune atlas were assessed by and classified using scTME, showing high concordance among immune subpopulations, with only two clear mismatches out of the 31 annotated cell types. c, Cells from the Han et al. TME atlas were classified by scTME, showing high concordance with all immune cells, as well as moderate concordance with fibroblast and endothelial populations, as annotated in their trained dataset and compared to the assessment of those same cells using the scTME program. d, Cells from the Abelson group’s scATOMIC cancer dataset were assessed and classified by the scTME R package, showing high correlation among immune populations and certain fibroblast subpopulations. a–d, Classification was performed using the scTME package against a 50,000-cell reference subset of the human atlas. In each panel, rows are the cell annotations supplied with the published dataset and columns are the scTME level 2 annotations; colour denotes the co-incidence of the two labellings.

a, c, CellChat evaluation of the VEGF (a) and ANGPT (c) signaling pathway networks. Left, heatmaps detailing the relative importance of individual cell populations as senders, receivers, mediators, and influencers. Dark green to black regions indicate strong signaling contributions, whereas light green to white regions indicate weaker signals. Blue arrows (and the blue box in panel a) highlight interactions of interest. Right, bar plots detailing the relative contribution of individual ligand-receptor pairs to the overall signaling pathway networks. b, d, NicheNet heatmaps of regulatory potential for macrophage/monocyte (Mac/Mono) (b) and mural cell (d) to ESM1+ tip cell signaling. The plots display prioritized sender ligands on the y-axis and their regulatory potential against predicted target genes on the x-axis.

a, b, UMAP embeddings of 1,000 sketched cells per study per integration technique (a) and projections of the sketched results from each integration approach onto all cells in the mouse atlas (b). c, Dot plots indicating expression levels of characteristic markers for each of the seven cell types. d, Venn diagrams showing overlap in cell annotations among each integration approach and the final atlas. e, f, Ratios of the number of cells in the intersection versus the union of Venn diagrams for each cell type in d (e), and the ratio of cells for each type included in the final atlas compared to those that would have been arrived at using the intersection (not union) of the three integration approaches (f). Notably, applying the intersection excludes many cells that may be desirable to include, whereas ratios greater than one in panel f indicate the presence of cells in the final atlas that would otherwise have been excluded using an intersectional approach. a, Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) embeddings of 2.5 million cells from 68 mouse studies integrated using Harmony, with consensus seven cell type annotations (outlined and labeled within panel) derived through multiple annotation approaches (Extended Data Figs. 1 and 8). Mykhailo Mudryk has revealed that he wanted to join Arsenal.

The Tottenham winger, on loan from Chelsea, admitted that before he signed for the Blues in January 2023, he had wanted to move to north London.

He made the switch from Shakhtar Dontesk in Ukraine for an initial £61million fee, that could rise to as high as £89m.

Before he made the move to Stamford Bridge, he had been heavily linked with a move to Mikel Arteta’s side, but ultimately, he decided to join Graham Potter’s Blues instead.

Now, he has declared that his real desire was a move to Arsenal, which never materialised.

“Before going to Chelsea, I wanted to join Arsenal. It’s no secret,” he told the Ukrainian podcast ‘Guest of Gordon’.

“Arsenal were the club I wanted to play for, and moving to the Emirates Stadium was my dream.

“There weren’t even any attempts to make my dream come true and move to Arsenal.

“The attempts from my previous agent were only to earn more money.

“But at the time, I didn’t know about it. I only understood about the commission and all the rest later on.”.

Mudryk reunited with his former Shakhtar boss Roberto De Zerbi at Spurs on Deadline Day in the summer transfer window, having been cleared to play after a doping ban for meldonium which began in October 2024.

The winger made headlines on Wednesday when he blamed his country’s football association for his positive drugs test, and ex-Chelsea striker and now-president of the Ukraine FA, Andriy Shevchenko, has demanded an apology from the 25-year-old.

Mudryk played just one match for the north Londoners - away at Nottingham Forest - before suffering a “stupid” ankle injury in training, according to his manager.

He is expected to return to action this weekend, however, when Spurs take on Ipswich Town at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, looking to get back to winning ways after a 1-0 defeat at Leeds before the international break.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Knapton | 20 Nov 2026 10:00.

Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta has revealed that Bukayo Saka will spend another four weeks on the sidelines with the quadriceps injury he sustained against Bayern Munich in the Champions League.

Saka's injury occurred in the first half of Arsenal's 2-2 draw with the Bundesliga champions on October 21, and Arteta immediately conceded at full time that the winger's problem looked severe.

Reports emerging soon after stated that Saka would miss between six and eight weeks, although Arsenal have been loath to put an exact timeframe on the Englishman's recovery just yet.

However, speaking to the media ahead of Saturday's Premier League clash with Newcastle United, Arteta admitted that Saka was only halfway into his recovery process and would spend the full eight weeks out.

"We had another test. It looks like it’s going to be an eight week injury more or less. He’s four weeks in now," the Spaniard told reporters.

Saka missing another four weeks means that the 25-year-old is set to sit out another seven matches across all competitions, including a number of heavyweight fixtures.

Arsenal host Borussia Dortmund in the Champions League next Tuesday, before ending the month with a clash of the titans against Manchester City in the Premier League.

Saka is also expected to miss matches with Brentford, Tottenham Hotspur and Real Madrid in early December, and he will most likely be unavailable for the visit of Bournemouth on December 13 too.

However, the attacker could be fit to make his comeback against Mauricio Pochettino's Manchester United on December 20, until when Noni Madueke and Max Dowman will provide cover.

Dowman will serve the third of his three-game domestic suspension against Newcastle this weekend, but Madueke has earned numerous plaudits in recent weeks, having scored against Slavia Prague in the Champions League before firing the effort that led to Martin Odegaard's winner against Hull City.

Saka will likely be one of two core members of Arsenal's title-winning team to miss matches against Tottenham and Real Madrid, as Arteta also delivered negative news on Martin Zubimendi.

The midfielder appeared to hurt his hamstring in Spain's 3-2 Nations League defeat to England during the international break, and he also faces around a month on the sidelines.

"He has a problem in his hamstring. The scan reveals there is an injury there he will be out for a few weeks," Arteta added on Zubimendi.

However, the 27-year-old is yet to start a Premier League game this season and was always expected to lose out to Declan Rice and Bruno Guimaraes at St James' Park tomorrow.

Arsenal are five points clear at the top of the Premier League table heading into gameweek 11 and are searching for their fourth successive win over Newcastle in the top flight.

Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada has insisted he was not involved ‘in any wrongdoings’ during his time at Manchester City amid the ongoing case against his former employers.

An independent commission found City guilty of breaching more than 100 of the Premier League’s financial rules in September between the period of 2009 and 2018.

City have appealed against the ruling and repeatedly denied any wrongdoing.

Berrada joined United in January 2024 having spent over a decade working in various roles for City Football Group.

He was named the club’s CEO in 2016 and remained in that role until 2020 when he was named City Football Group’s chief football operations officer for the next four years.

Sources indicate that berrada’s time at the club’s CEO overlaps with the period in which City were investigated. But the United chief has no concerns over any implications for him in the case.

‘I’m not concerned,’ Berrada told Sky Sports.

Recent findings suggest that ‘I want to be very clear about this: I wasn’t involved in any wrongdoings. I wasn’t involved in the proceedings. There are no allegations against me.

‘In that sense, there will be no surprises.’.

Asked whether United could look to pursue compensation if City fail in their appeal, Berrada replied: ‘I don’t want to comment on that because right now, it’s an ongoing process.

‘When it runs its course, then we’ll take a view on what is our position as Manchester United.’.

Berrada and the rest of United’s hierarchy have just presided over their third mid-season managerial sacking in three years with Mauricio Pochettino the latest to be tasked with lifting the club from its malaise.

‘If you think about the fact that we’ve had three permanent managers in less than three seasons, clearly we haven’t achieved the stability that we want to – that’s for sure,’ Berrada noted.

‘There are different circumstances as to why it didn’t work out with Erik, Ruben and now Michael. And we’re always learning. We’re always trying to improve and understand what has failed.’.

Manchester United’s CEO Omar Berrada has hit back at criticism of the club’s transfer strategy last summer and insists a ‘disciplined’ approach is required.

United spent £155 million on signing three midfielders in Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba in the summer transfer window.

However, Mauricio Pochettino arrives at Old Trafford this week without a recognised striker as Benjamin Sesko is out for the remainder of the year with a shin problem, while Luke Shaw has missed United’s last seven games due to injury.

United supporters have criticised the club’s decision to only strengthen Michael Carrick’s midfield in the summer but Berrada is adamant the squad is ‘fundamentally better’ after their signings.

‘You have to take it in the context of the last few years,’ Berrada told Sky Sports.

Industry observers note that ‘The summer of 2025, I think the recruitment team was widely praised with the four players that were signed. And they did very well. They helped the team achieve Champions League qualification.

‘When we look at this summer, we went in knowing what we needed to do. Of course, there have been different dynamics at play. It’s probably been the summer or the transfer window where there’s been the highest inflation in transfer fees.

According to recent reports, ‘And we’ve stated publicly and we’ve said consistently in the last few years that we need to stay disciplined. We need to take the right decisions. We need to buy the right players for the right value at the right time in terms of what the squad needs.

‘And when we look at the summer transfer window of 2026, I know we’re receiving a lot of criticism for it but we’re actually happy with the players that we bought.

‘We think that Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Karl Darlow, and let’s not forget that we’ve also welcomed back Marcus Rashford, who had a very good season on loan at Barcelona – these are five additions that we think have made the squad fundamentally better.

Sources indicate that ‘It’s true that we lost Casemiro, who is a top player and gave a lot to the club. We also lost Manuel Ugarte to, unfortunately, an ACL injury. So our focus was very much about straightening the midfield.

According to recent reports, ‘When we started the transfer window, we really only had Kobbie Mainoo as our midfielder. So we wanted to reinforce that, and we did it.’.

Berrada also addressed United’s decision not to sign a fresh left-sided defender after the club made an enquiry for Newcastle United’s Lewis Hall in the summer.

‘When you look at the other areas of the pitch, and there’s a lot of discussion about the back line,’ Berrada said.

‘But we did come into it thinking we have depth. We have nine players that can play in the back line, in the back four positions.

‘So that’s why we looked primarily at investing in the midfield. But we were always looking for opportunities. I think it’s been widely reported that we were looking at potentially the left-back position as a reinforcement.

Industry observers note that ‘I think what we’ve seen in the back line is we’ve had injuries, it’s taken Matthijs de Ligt longer than we would want it to get back. Unfortunately, Luke Shaw suffered a muscle injury that meant he was out for five or six weeks.

‘So could we have signed an additional defender to straighten the depth and the quality? Yes, but we have to find the right players and you have to find the right players at the right value.

‘There’s no point in us spending £40 million, £50m for players that we’re not convinced are going to add value to the team.

‘So it’s always about being disciplined and finding the right opportunities and getting the right players that are going to take us forward.

‘When I talk about being disciplined, I talk about not overspending on players that don’t necessarily add quality to the team.

In a recent development, ‘Because when you sign a player that doesn’t work out for Man Utd, it becomes very difficult to move that player on or to get the sale we want. And that can set us back.

Recent findings suggest that ‘So when I talk about being disciplined, I’m not talking about necessarily not spending to get the top players. We have the ambition to win, to win the Premier League, to win the Champions League, to win the domestic cups. And for that, we need top talent. So when we find the right opportunities, we will spend. But what we don’t want to be doing is spending just for the sake of it.’.

By CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER.

Manchester United have expressed their concern over the circumstances surrounding JJ Gabriel’s imminent move to Real Madrid, and threatened legal action if there is any evidence that he was induced to leave.

The 16-year-old winger posted a video on social media on Tuesday night confirming his departure from United as talks with Madrid continue between his upcoming agent Ali Barat and close family at the club’s Valdebebas headquarters.

United sources say they are disappointed the video appeared without any contact with them, but the club will maintain its policy of not punishing Gabriel for what it sees as the actions of adults.

However, they have reiterated that United will fight with every legal means possible if any evidence of inducement from another club comes to light.

It’s understood that United have been unable to make contact with Gabriel – who has not been seen at the club since September – or his family despite numerous attempts to check on his welfare. They want an opportunity to ensure that he has a say in what could be a life-changing decision.

Gabriel has been training in Madrid and gave an interview to Marca earlier this month saying that he favoured a move to the 15-time European champions over rivals Barcelona, while expressing an ambition to win the Ballon d’Or.

Manchester United are prepared for a legal fight with Real Madrid over JJ Gabriel.

The youngster is on the verge of joining the Spanish giants in a controversial move.

He is registered as a United player for the rest of the season and the club are refusing to tear up that agreement in the belief that he would still need approval from FIFA to make the move. However, sources stress that there has been no contact from any football authority seeking to de-register him.

Gabriel has been at United since the age of 11, and is considered one of the hottest young prospects in European football. He is registered with United's academy until the end of the season but Real Madrid are intending to sign him in January.

There is a FIFA loophole that allows European clubs to tie down young players to professional contracts if they have a European passport which Gabriel qualifies for through both parents.

In a farewell post on Instagram he said: 'Dear Manchester United, I arrived in 2020. as a 10-year-old boy with substantial dreams.

Industry observers note that 'Here I grew as a player and as a person. From scoring at Old Trafford to receiving the Jimmy Murphy Award.

'You gave me moments I'll always treasure. To every coach, every member of staff, to my team-mates and everyone who supported me, thank you for believing in me and helping me grow.

Recent findings suggest that 'As I begin my next chapter, Manchester United will always be a part of my story. Thank you for everything. JJ.'.

Gabriel did not make a competitive first-team appearance for United, but did make a senior appearance in United's pre-season friendly defeat to AC Milan this summer.

United’s hierarchy were left unsure what triggered his request to leave given he had become a key part of plans in first team training sessions this season.

United were left rocked in September when Gabriel's family unexpectedly requested to cancel his contract with immediate effect.

Daily Mail Sport revealed at the time that United’s hierarchy were left unsure what triggered such a move given he had become a key part of plans in first team training sessions this season under Michael Carrick.

Industry observers note that A week later, Daily Mail Sport revealed that the decline of United since the days of Sir Alex Ferguson was the driving force behind Gabriel's family seeking an exit. United have not won a Premier League title since 2013.

A source close to the family explained that United are 'far away' from the likes of Barcelona, Real Madrid, Bayern Munich, as well as domestic rivals Arsenal and Manchester City, and that they want him to 'learn from the best' to maximise his talents.

'His dad has ambitions for his son to be the best in the world and play with the best and learn from the best and right now that's not current situation at United - far from it,' a source explained.

He has not been seen at the club since he scored a hat-trick for the Under 21s on his UEFA Youth League debut against Sabah.

England will face Norway in the Nations League quarter-finals, and they could lock horns with a familiar foe in the last four should they make it.

It will be the first time that Thomas Tuchel’s side have played the Scandinavians since the World Cup quarter-finals, where England won out 2-1 in Miami, Florida thanks to a brace from Jude Bellingham after Andreas Schjelderup’s stunning opener.

The Three Lions found out their opponents in Friday’s knockout-stage draw, which took place at UEFA’s headquarters in Nyon, Switzerland.

Tuchel’s men finished top of Group A after a stunning 3-2 victory over world champions Spain in Madrid last weekend.

Luis de la Fuente’s European champions, meanwhile, will take on France in their last-eight clash, with the European giants set to face off for the first time since the World Cup semi-final, where La Roja emerged 2-0 winners thanks to Mikel Oyarzabal and Pedro Porro’s goals.

The remaining two fixtures are the Netherlands against Portugal, and Belgium facing Germany.

The four quarter-finals will take place in March next year, with the winners going through to the finals in June next year.

The semi-finals were also revealed, with England on a collision course with historic rivals Germany, should the Three Lions get through Norway and Jurgen Klopp’s men beat Belgium.

The victors of Spain vs France will take on the winners between the Netherlands and Portugal.

Galatasaray striker Victor Osimhen would be open to joining Manchester United next summer, according to reports.

United are expected to be in the market to sign a new striker within the next two transfer windows due to their shortage of options in attack.

Mauricio Pochettino arrived at United this week with Benjamin Sesko sidelined until next year due to a shin injury, while Joshua Zirkzee has scored just 11 goals in 85 appearances since his £36.5 million move to Old Trafford in 2024.

Osimhen, meanwhile, is also out of action after undergoing knee surgery earlier this month but Galatasaray are hoping that the Nigeria international will return before the end of December.

The 27-year-old is in his third season with Galatasaray after the Turkish club made his loan move permanent for €75m (£64.8m) last year.

Osimhen has thrived during his time in Turkey, scoring 69 goals in 84 appearances for Galatasaray.

According to The Sun, Osimhen is keen on playing in the Premier League before the end of his career and the striker would be open to joining United if the opportunity arises.

The report claims that Osimhen’s camp have been made aware of United’s renewed interest.

‘Of course the interest really flatters him but he’s a loyal guy so it will be up to United to move hard for him,’ a source close to Osimhen told the newspaper.

Carlo Pellegatti has painted a positive picture regarding AC Milan’s developments, one that puts last season’s collapse into perspective.

Rewinding to the end of May, it felt like Milan’s entire world have caved in. A 2-1 defeat at home to Cagliari – a game that they led in early on – in the final round of the season condemned the Rossoneri to a fifth-placed finish, meaning they missed out on Champions League football again.

In a recent development, this is after Massimiliano Allegri had the team in a title fight going into the Spring, but ultimately the decline was near-vertical towards the end of the campaign. He paid the price for this, as did the CEO Giorgio Furlani, sporting director Igli Tare and chief scout Geoffrey Moncada.

In his latest column for MilanNews, Carlo Pellegatti has put forward the notion that the defeat to the Sardinians might turn out to be a blessing. Why? Because the reset that followed on a sporting and managerial level seems to already be taking a positive shape.

“Krosche and delight! It’s a somewhat obvious joke, but it captures the expectations of AC Milan fans. When will he arrive? November 27th, as I’ve been told, or in the first ten days of December, or even – I really hope not – January 1st?” he began.

“The difference in dates for the announcement of his newly introduced role is by no means insignificant, because the January transfer window becomes a crucial turning point for Milan’s fortunes, both today and in the future.

“The sooner the Head of Football sits down at Casa Milan, the better he can weave his web to strengthen the team in the winter transfer window. This should have been the job of a year ago, but was not accomplished by a shortsighted management team that never understood the difference between costs and investments.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s also a shame that Igli Tare is a person who respects roles and is attentive to internal balances. He had to, and this is his great regret, bypass those who managed Milan, to speak with Gerry Cardinale and explain the importance of the arrival of a striker and a defender, who would have allowed them to be in the Champions League today.

“I’m using a very bold paradox, one I’ve never admitted. If failing to qualify for the Champions League was the reason that pushed Gerry Cardinale to fire the key figures of the three worst and most disastrous years in Milan’s history, then, given the exciting future prospects, it would have been better to lose against Cagliari, which avoided prolonging the agony of our dear old AC Milan. A painful sacrifice that, I hope, will be repaid with success in the years to come.

“With a Cardinale who was too absent and distant, guilty, by his own admission, of having delegated the management of his club to unsuitable people, but who now becomes the protagonist of this new way of operating, reminiscent of the good old days.

“I obviously feel sorry for Tare and Allegri, who, despite having their responsibilities, were victims of a confusing, chaotic, and divisive situation, and through no fault of their own.

It has been revealed that “Returning to Krosche, I hope he promptly finds his feet in this Milan adventure that awaits him. I continue to believe that a highly experienced and highly skilled Italian operative, to work alongside the German director, could and can be of help to him and Milan, given the obvious difficulties of integrating into a world that is completely different from the German one.

Industry observers note that “Gerry Cardinale and his chief assistant, Massimo Calvelli, are convinced of the wisdom of their choice, after meeting several times with Markus Krosche. I think it’s crucial that he’s not only a skilled market operator, but also a valid on-field contact for Ruben Amorim.

Industry observers note that “The Portuguese will then be able to discuss potential choices and decisions with his Head of Football. In short, it was a position in the organisational chart that was culpably neglected, with the results that were seen, until Gerry Cardinale himself imposed Igli Tare, who, in any case, did not have an easy job.

Industry observers note that “I mentioned Massimo Calvelli, who, in the media, always appears to be somewhat out of the spotlight. Certainly not in operational terms, because, from what I know, he was the absolute protagonist and architect of transactions that brought approximately €825m into Milan’s coffers.

“He was certainly a skilled architect of the return of Adidas as a shirt sponsor, but also a key figure in the acquisition of Generali, which will give its name to the new stadium, this time with the collaboration, it is mentioned, of Paolo Scaroni.

By Darren Plant | 20 Nov 2026 10:04.

Burnley play host to rivals Blackburn Rovers looking for the win that would ensure that they avoid being cut adrift in the relegation zone.

At a time when the Clarets sit in 22nd position in the Championship table, Rovers return after the international break in 13th place.

When Burnley stormed into a 4-1 lead at Cardiff City earlier this month, Fabio Celestini would have been confident that he was recording his first win as head coach that would also kick-start the club's season.

Instead, a 29-minute capitulation that resulted in a 5-4 defeat in South Wales has left relegation feeling increasingly likely, even though the season is only just under a third of the way complete.

Burnley remain on 10 points from 15 matches, their only success coming at fellow strugglers Watford, and they are already five points adrift of safety.

Although an upturn in fortunes would see them quickly haul themselves back into contention to avoid the drop, conceding 31 goals - the worst defensive record in the Championship - will not fill supporters with confidence.

Five of Burnley's seven Championship games at Turf Moor this season have ended in draws, but they remain the only team in the division without a home victory.

As for Blackburn, they have an interim management team in place after Tony Mowbray stood down from his position earlier this week due to health complications.

Rovers sit 11 points above their fierce rivals in the standings, the pre-season expectation having been that the points difference would be close to the exact opposite at this stage of the campaign.

Nevertheless, Blackburn have won five of their last nine fixtures in the second tier to keep them in the hunt for a playoff spot.

The 2-1 victory over West Ham United in their last outing made it five wins from eight matches at Ewood Park.

However, Rovers have prevailed in just one of their seven away fixtures, a 1-0 success at Bristol City on October 13.

Blackburn Rovers Championship form:.

Celestini will inevitably make changes to his Burnley XI, with Max Alleyne and Josh Cullen among those who could return in defence and midfield.

Goalkeeper Max Weiss may potentially be handed a recall between the sticks in place of Gregoire Coubert, while Zeki Amdouni could start on the left flank.

However, Connor Roberts starts a three-game ban, a consequence of an incident at the end of the Cardiff game that led to retrospective punishment.

Despite Damien Johnson and Mike Dodds taking the reins from Mowbray, the Blackburn XI will look similar from the victory over West Ham.

However, second-choice goalkeeper Aynsley Pears is expected to deputise for Balazs Toth, who suffered a finger injury while on international duty with Hungary.

If the likes of Mathias Jorgensen and Ryoya Morishita overcome injuries in time for this fixture, they will likely be named on the substitutes' bench at best.

Burnley possible starting lineup:.

Weiss; Walker, Ekdal, Alleyne, Pires; Hatate, Cullen; Ramazani, Edwards, Amdouni; Hountondji.

Blackburn Rovers possible starting lineup:.

Pears; Beyuku, Carter, McLoughlin, Pickering; Morsy, Montgomery; Fevrier, Cantwell, Afolayan; Gudjohnsen.

According to recent reports, with Burnley struggling for wins and Blackburn having to adapt with Mowbray in charge, this points to a game where both teams would be happy to avoid a defeat. Therefore, we anticipate a low-scoring draw being played out at Turf Moor.

England will face Norway in the Nations League quarter-finals, and they could lock horns with a familiar foe in the last four should they make it.

It will be the first time that Thomas Tuchel’s side have played the Scandinavians since the World Cup quarter-finals, where England won out 2-1 in Miami, Florida thanks to a brace from Jude Bellingham after Andreas Schjelderup’s stunning opener.

The Three Lions found out their opponents in Friday’s knockout-stage draw, which took place at UEFA’s headquarters in Nyon, Switzerland.

Tuchel’s men finished top of Group A after a stunning 3-2 victory over world champions Spain in Madrid last weekend.

Luis de la Fuente’s European champions, meanwhile, will take on France in their last-eight clash, with the European giants set to face off for the first time since the World Cup semi-final, where La Roja emerged 2-0 winners thanks to Mikel Oyarzabal and Pedro Porro’s goals.

The remaining two fixtures are the Netherlands against Portugal, and Belgium facing Germany.

The four quarter-finals will take place in March next year, with the winners going through to the finals in June next year.

The semi-finals were also revealed, with England on a collision course with historic rivals Germany, should the Three Lions get through Norway and Jurgen Klopp’s men beat Belgium.

The victors of Spain vs France will take on the winners between the Netherlands and Portugal.

Netherlands/Portugal vs Spain/France.

Norway/England vs Belgium/Germany.

Antonio Conte has played down suggestions he missed out on the Manchester United job because of his demanding reputation in management.

United made their third mid-season managerial change in three years after sacking Michael Carrick with Mauricio Pochettino coming in as his replacement earlier this month.

Sources indicate that conte was among the names initially explored along with Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann. The Italian, a free agent since parting ways with Napoli, was thought to be keen on the role at Old Trafford but it was widely reported United had reservations over some of his methods.

The Italian led Juventus, Chelsea, Inter Milan and Napoli to league titles but has not lasted longer than two seasons at any club since leaving the Bianconeri in 2014.

Conte has a reputation for being hugely demanding with players and the board but in an interview with Cronache di Spogliatoio he insisted anyone scared of his approach is scared of winning.

The coach recalled a meeting with Sir Alex Ferguson during his time in charge of Chelsea, praising the standards the Scot said before insisting the idea United no longer want to meet those standards is ‘offensive’.

‘If someone is scared of my method, then they’re scared of winning, because that methodology leads to winning,’ Conte remarked.

Sources indicate that ‘That’s my answer. United has such an notable history that it seems strange to imagine anyone being scared of a job aimed at restoring the club to its former glory.

They last won the championship in 2013, under Ferguson. I have enormous respect for Sir Alex Ferguson. I’ve read his book, and when I was in London, I was lucky enough to go to his house and spend a day with him. He’s incredibly eager to talk about football, even if it’s sometimes hard to understand his Scottish accent.

‘If you then tell me that it’s a method that needs work, I’d say yes: everyone needs to work, not just the players.’.

Manchester United have been left red-faced after a drone covertly filmed Mauricio Pochettino’s first training session and posted the footage to YouTube.

The Argentine, who signed up to replace Michael Carrick as United’s head coach last week, arrived at Carrington on Wednesday to start work with his new club.

With United languishing in the drop zone, Pochettino faces a brutal opening fixture of his reign, away at Liverpool.

But his preparations for that match have already been compromised in a concerning security breach at United’s training centre, after a drone secretly recorded 12 minutes of Pochettino’s first session with the club, with footage posted on YouTube for all to see.

The drone does not appear to have entered Carrington’s airspace at any point, but footage filmed with a zoom lens shows the session in clear detail.

The YouTube channel which posted the clip followed it up with a statement claiming they had broken no laws by recording the session as the airspace around Carrington is unrestricted.

No players or staff caught in the footage appeared to be aware of the fact they were being filmed. At the time of writing, the clip has accrued over 40,000 views.

In a recent development, the footage indicates the United squad working in two groups. One was being put through a rondo on one pitch, while Pochettino led the other through what appeared to be a tactical session on another. Both groups appeared to comprise a blend of first-team and academy players.

Manchester United declined to comment when contacted by Standard Sport.

EU moves to loosen rules on pesticide use as experts sound the alarm

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1171 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As part of its drive to "streamline and simplify" EU laws, the European Commission has proposed sweeping changes for agriculture and food safety legislation.
  • Under current EU rules, which date back to 2011, primary pesticide components, or active substances, are only granted approval for limited periods of no more than 15 years.
  • Sources indicate that the European Commission's proposed revamp of the system would make indefinite greenlighting — including of the controversial glyphosate, which has been linked to cancer and kills almost all plant life — the default.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As part of its drive to "streamline and simplify" EU laws, the European Commission has proposed sweeping changes for agriculture and food safety legislation. These include a move to ease rules controlling the use of pesticides and herbicides, which help fight pests and weeds.

Under current EU rules, which date back to 2011, primary pesticide components, or active substances, are only granted approval for limited periods of no more than 15 years.

Sources indicate that the European Commission's proposed revamp of the system would make indefinite greenlighting — including of the controversial glyphosate, which has been linked to cancer and kills almost all plant life — the default. Safety reviews would only be done in exceptional cases, and regulatory authorities, not the industry, would bear responsibility.

Recent findings suggest that the commission has mentioned its goal is to cut costs, simplify work for authorities and help farmers stay competitive. Scientists and doctors, however, warn that concerns over human health and environmental impact from these toxic substances are being brushed aside.

The European Commission has remarked it's responding to complaints from farmers and the agriculture industry to clarify EU rules that govern pesticide use.

A joint statement released in May by 19 food associations, including CropLife Europe, which promotes pesticides, said complicated administrative procedures and a lengthy approvals process meant farmers were "left without any effective solutions to protect their crops against insects, weeds and diseases," putting food security and livelihoods at risk.

"The existing system of periodic renewal assessment of every active substance has become unsustainable," the commission's press service told DW, citing "chronic delays" and "bottlenecks" in the approval of latest, more sustainable products.

In recent negotiations, EU member states stated open-ended authorizations should be restricted to "low-risk active substances.".

But their stance is still wanting to extend initial approval periods for other substances to up to 15 years, and a maximum of 25 years for renewals.

Herbert Dorfmann, a center-right Italian member of the European Parliament, noted there is currently a yearslong delay in approving new pesticides, including more eco-friendly options, meaning farmers are forced to rely on older substances. Or, if these are banned, go without altogether.

The commission wants to "make the system more efficient and responsive," while guaranteeing that "the protection of human and animal health and the environment remain the highest priorities.".

Dorfmann, who as co-rapporteur is responsible for interinstitutional negotiations on the issue, backs the commission's stance, saying the EU needs "to open up the system for innovation.".

He aims to bring the parliament's proposal on the new pesticide rules to a vote among EU lawmakers before the end of the year.

Ecologists and medical experts, however, have spoken out forcefully against the proposed changes, saying the potential implications for human health and the environment are being downplayed.

In September, more than 500 experts from across the EU signed an open letter calling on the European Parliament to suspend its consideration of the new regulations and conduct an independent investigation into health and environmental impacts.

On October 7, UN rights experts also backed the call for a full review into whether the proposed changes violated the EU's obligations under international human rights law, especially with regard to agricultural workers and children.

Pesticides can persist in the environment, contaminating water and degrading soils. They can also drive biodiversity loss and poison other animals higher up the food chain.

When it comes to humans, the European Environment Agency has mentioned it was "not yet possible to estimate the burden of disease linked to current levels of exposure to all pesticides.".

However, exposure to chemical pesticides, including banned substances that still persist in the environment, has been linked to various cancers, chronic respiratory disease, neurological disorders and developmental delays, as well as problems with fertility and behavior.

And exposure is widespread: A survey conducted between 2014 and 2021 found that 84% of urine samples from both children and adults in five European countries contained residue from two or more pesticides.

Martina Vijver, scientific director and ecotoxicology expert at Leiden University in the Netherlands, said experts were "deeply concerned" that the EU's current plan "will weaken rather than strengthen the level of protection for pesticide regulation.".

Speaking at the European Parliament in September, she mentioned regular reassessments were key to evaluating the safety of pesticides with fresh findings, pointing out that the perception of risk changes over time.

"The regulatory system must remain capable of correcting yesterday's decisions with tomorrow's knowledge," she said.

Salome Roynel, a policy officer at the Pesticide Action Network Europe, an NGO based in Brussels, said the harmful effects of pesticides aren't often fully understood until years later, when the product is up for reconsideration.

"Latest science emerges all the time," she told DW, highlighting how 56 active substances have been banned in the EU since 2011 as a result of periodic reviews.

That includes the insecticide chlorpyrifos, previously used in orchards and on vegetable and cereal crops, which has been tied to harmful effects on children's brain development.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Roynel said it was "obvious that there was some kind of alignment" between the changes proposed by the EU institutions and the demands of the pesticide lobby.

This echoes a new report by nonprofit research and campaign group Corporate Europe Observatory, which mentioned Dorfmann and other lawmakers had "copy-pasted […] industry demands" into their regulatory proposals.

Dorfmann denied the lobby influence, telling DW he had met with "both sides, industry and environmental associations," in public debates on the issue.

In a recent development, "The main objective is not to keep old products in the market. The main objective is to bring upcoming ones to the market," Dorfmann noted.

Part of that plan, he added, would be to help more environmentally friendly "biocontrol" products and low-risk substances to bypass current administrative hurdles and get on the market faster.

It's an idea previously championed by Vijver, who agrees that the current system means more environmentally friendly pesticides are stuck in an administrative "traffic jam." She told DW that biocontrol products could go in a green "bus lane" to ease the way to approval at the European Food Safety Authority, while maintaining crucial safety reviews to filter out the more dangerous products.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Roynel also supports the strategy to speed up approval for biocontrol substances, but noted it needs to be part of a wider system change that includes financial support, monitoring and training to use these new products, as well as maintaining the restrictions on more harmful chemical pesticides ― not further deregulation.

Sources indicate that "If farmers get easier access to synthetic pesticides tomorrow, they would have no incentive to switch to biocontrol," she remarked. "It's vital to put [biocontrol pesticides] on the market and we fully support that, but… it will not be the silver bullet.".

Boca Juniors, under Rodolfo Arruabarrena, have won their last six matches, four of them without conceding, and head into the final in considerably better form, one that also carries a place in the 2027 Copa Libertadores group stage and the next Recopa Sudamericana.

Atletico Mineiro built their Copa Sudamericana campaign on six wins, two draws and four defeats, scoring 18 goals and conceding 14. Topping Group B secured a direct route into the last 16.

It has been revealed that in the knockout rounds, Atletico Mineiro faced contrasting scenarios. They eliminated RB Bragantino 3-2 on aggregate, fought back in Belo Horizonte after losing the first leg to Santos, and confirmed their place on penalties following a dramatic tie.

The semi-final again highlighted that inconsistency. Atletico Mineiro built a 3-0 lead over Montevideo City Torque at the Arena MRV and, despite losing 2-0 in Uruguay, held on to progress thanks to the cushion from the first leg.

Recent findings suggest that the main concern is recent form. Since their last Brasileirao win, Atletico Mineiro have picked up five defeats and two draws, scored just three goals in that spell, and failed to find the net in five of those seven matches.

In a recent development, that slump adds to the emotional weight of the two continental finals Atletico Mineiro have already lost in recent seasons, to Botafogo in the 2024 Copa Libertadores and to Lanus in the 2025 Copa Sudamericana. Boca Juniors dropped into the Copa Sudamericana after finishing third in their Copa Libertadores group. Since then, they have rebuilt their campaign, winning five, drawing one and losing two in the knockout phase, scoring 13 goals and conceding just five.

It has been revealed that their run began with a penalty-shootout win over O’Higgins and gained momentum in the last 16, when they beat Recoleta home and away. In the quarter-finals, they managed the advantage built at home and eliminated Sao Paulo with a draw in Brazil.

The semi-final demanded a stronger response. Having been beaten by Vasco da Gama at La Bombonera, Boca Juniors turned the tie around at the Maracana, showing they could raise their level when needing a result away from home.

Recent findings suggest that recent form backs up that improvement. Boca Juniors have won six matches in a row across all competitions, scoring 11 goals and conceding just two, a run that combines sharper finishing with a more settled defence. They also arrive on the back of the Liga Argentina title, secured with a stoppage-time Enner Valencia goal in a win over Defensa y Justicia on November 7.

Against Brazilian sides in continental competition in 2026, Boca Juniors have two wins, two draws and two defeats, with six goals scored and five conceded. In the overall head-to-head, the Argentines hold the edge, but Atletico Mineiro have won the two most recent knockout meetings between the clubs, adding some balance to the final’s history.

#14620. Can we regrow damaged seagrass meadows?

Can we regrow damaged seagrass meadows?

📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (787 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, half a dozen divers are navigating the cold waters of the Baltic Sea off the coast of Dahme, a small beach town in northern Germany.
  • They only take a few shoots from each spot, which will be planted where the conservationists hope to regrow another meadow.
  • The scientists see the work as critical.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, half a dozen divers are navigating the cold waters of the Baltic Sea off the coast of Dahme, a small beach town in northern Germany. Keeping the roots intact, conservationists carefully lift shoots from a donor meadow of seagrass and place them in a bag.

They only take a few shoots from each spot, which will be planted where the conservationists hope to regrow another meadow. They've already picked out a prime area for the young plants, which need sandy sediment, shelter from waves and currents and sufficient light and oxygen to thrive.

The scientists see the work as critical. Myriam Spicka, who heads the NGO Seagrass Conservation, indicates she has "seen the changes" in the more than 30 years she's been diving. And she is not the only one who has witnessed the destruction.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Scientists estimate that around 60% of the Baltic coast's seagrass meadows have disappeared.

It has been revealed that "That's the bad news," said marine ecologist Thorsten Reusch from the GEOMAR Helmholtz Center for Ocean Research Kiel . "The good news is that the decline has stopped.".

It has been revealed that underwater seagrass meadows feed and shelter fish, crabs, shellfish and many other species. They improve water quality and slow waves, helping protect shores from erosion. And they store carbon in the seabed about 30 to 50 times faster than forests.

It has been revealed that around 70 species of seagrass can be found along the coasts of more than 150 countries. Some grow just below the surface, others at depths of 60 meters or almost 200 feet.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

"Some countries have far more seagrass, particularly in the Indo-Pacific," said Reusch. "There, it can play a major role in their carbon balance.".

But the value of seagrass goes beyond carbon storage. Its meadows in the Baltic are among the sea's most valuable habitats. They shelter wildlife, stabilize the seabed and act as natural filters by trapping particles and nutrients.

Planting individual seagrass shoots is painstaking work so people like Reinhard Helbig are trying to make it easier.

Through ZosteraTec, the start-up he co-founded, he helps restore marine habitats, including seagrass meadows damaged by offshore activity, such as wind farm construction. His work begins on the beach.

"Stormy weather helps us. Waves and currents wash seagrass out of the seabed. A day or two later, it washes up here, still fresh," he stated.

The collected shoots are grown and multiplied in ZosteraTec's aquaculture. Several months later, the marine saplings are laid on a plant support. A specially developed machine binds the planted strands with biodegradable thread. The resulting lengths can be laid on the seabed with less diving work.

Recent findings suggest that "We plant here on land to cut down on underwater work. That means fewer dives, and we can do the painstaking work on shore," Helbig stated.

Researchers at the Geomar Helmholtz Center in Kiel are also testing fresh ways to restore seagrass across larger areas, including using seeds.

Marine ecologist Esther Thomsen reaches into an aquarium tank and pulls out a flowerpot containing seagrass.

"Ten percent of the plants in our meadows produce seeds. You can clearly see the seeds sitting inside the seed pod," she said.

"The substantial advantage of restoring meadows from seed is greater genetic diversity. And in the future, we should be able to sow seeds over much larger areas," explained Thomsen.

Reusch from Geomar stated they at the moment "think the most promising way to grow meadows that can withstand climate change is to plant individual shoots as a foundation, then sow seeds between them to increase genetic diversity.".

Whether a planting mission is successful is revealed months or even years later.

Recent findings suggest that thomsen and her colleagues are visiting the first seagrass meadow planted in Germany's Baltic waters in 2021. The divers count shoots, check how densely they grow and record how the meadow has developed.

According to recent reports, they then compare it with the donor meadow that supplied the plants. Only that comparison reveals whether the fresh crop has merely survived or is beginning to function more like a natural one.

It has been revealed that "We've just checked the seagrass meadow, and it's really dense. We counted lots of shoots per square," Thomsen noted. "It's looking really good.".

This article is based on a Global Us video report.

MATCH PREDICTION – REAL MADRID WIN.

Madrid have lost just one of their last 24 LaLiga games against Celta (W21 D2), a 2-0 defeat in December 2025, winning 11 of the last 12.

Los Blancos have won their last eight games in all competitions, their best winning run since a 10-game streak between May and September 2022 under Carlo Ancelotti.

However, Madrid lost their last home game against Celta in LaLiga and have only twice lost consecutive home games against them in the competition (L2 in 1943 and in 2006).

Celta have picked up points in six of their last seven away games against teams from the Community of Madrid in LaLiga (W3 D3 L1), but they lost their most recent such match 3-0 against Rayo Vallecano last October.

Celta have conceded 10 goals and kept six clean sheets in LaLiga 2026-27, both their best records after the first 12 games of a season in the competition since 2002-03 (eight goals and seven clean sheets), under Miguel Angel Lotina.

A glucose-powered artificial neuroimmune axis for metabolic control

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 58 min read (11610 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~58 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that metabolic disorders such as diabetes mellitus are global health crises driven by metabolic imbalance, chronic inflammation and dysfunction of the neuroimmune axis1,2,3.
  • According to recent reports, diabetes mellitus and associated metabolic disorders are major public health challenges, affecting more than 14% of the total adult population worldwide10,11.
  • Despite the neuroimmune axis being a promising therapeutic target for diabetes mellitus17, developing a therapeutic strategy to restore its impaired function remains a daunting challenge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that metabolic disorders such as diabetes mellitus are global health crises driven by metabolic imbalance, chronic inflammation and dysfunction of the neuroimmune axis1,2,3. Electroceuticals targeting the autonomic nervous system have shown anti-inflammatory effects, yet existing systems lack the metabolic interoceptive feedback to fully restore immune–metabolic homeostasis4,5,6,7,8,9. Here we report an artificial neuroimmune axis (NeuroAxis) as a closed-loop immunomodulatory therapy for treating metabolic diseases. Analogous to its biological counterpart, NeuroAxis is solely powered by endogenous glucose, operating without batteries or wireless power transfer. It emulates the vagal reflex through closed-loop neuromodulation with metabolic interoceptive feedback. In a rat model of type 1 diabetes, NeuroAxis promotes the recovery of insulin-producing pancreatic β-cells and reduces inflammatory immune responses; in a rat model of type 2 diabetes, it drives macrophage remodelling and reduces systemic chronic inflammation. In both models, NeuroAxis restores glucose tolerance, improves insulin sensitivity and normalizes glycaemic control, with therapeutic effects persisting after treatment cessation. Our artificial neuroimmune axis promotes substantial advances in treating metabolic disorders and represents a general approach for autonomously regulating interorgan communication, central to homeostasis and pathophysiology.

According to recent reports, diabetes mellitus and associated metabolic disorders are major public health challenges, affecting more than 14% of the total adult population worldwide10,11. Beyond hyperglycaemia, these conditions are often accompanied by chronic inflammation and impaired coordination between the nervous, immune and metabolic systems, resulting in maladaptive autonomic responses and an impaired neuroimmune axis3,10,11,12. In particular, the vagus nerve, a bidirectional conduit linking afferent metabolic signals to efferent autonomic output, critically governs metabolic tone12. Under hyperglycaemic conditions, parasympathetic vagal activation reduces hepatic glucose output and increases pancreatic insulin secretion6,13. Moreover, vagal signalling modulates immune function through the inflammatory reflex, whereby efferent vagus nerve activity can suppress inflammation by attenuating pro-inflammatory cytokine release across diverse conditions2,14,15,16. Preclinical and clinical evidence indicates that electrical stimulation of the vagus nerve can suppress systemic inflammation, improve insulin sensitivity and augment pancreatic β-cell activity6,12,13.

Despite the neuroimmune axis being a promising therapeutic target for diabetes mellitus17, developing a therapeutic strategy to restore its impaired function remains a daunting challenge. The challenge arises from the lack of afferent vagal nerve functions in real-time sensing of metabolic cues (for example, glucose concentration). Recent advances in artificial nerves have led to the restoration of the impaired sensorimotor loop. However, the artificial afferent nerves are designed to sense physical input (for example, pressure) from the environment, rather than metabolic signals within the body18,19. Similarly, feedback with indirect surrogate biomarkers, such as heart rate variability, gastric motility or electroencephalographic activity, is unable to restore the neuroimmune axis4,5,20,21,22, resulting in suboptimal clinical outcomes and adverse effects such as bradycardia or gastrointestinal symptoms5,23,24. Moreover, continuous electrochemical sensing in implantable electronics introduces additional system-level challenges, including sustained electrical biasing, low-noise signal amplification and wireless data transmission25,26, which collectively increase energy demand and system complexity, thereby limiting the development of compact, long-term and self-sustained closed-loop neuromodulation systems.

Recent findings suggest that to address these challenges, we developed NeuroAxis, which uses glucose as both an endogenous energy source and an interoceptive metabolic signal to restore the impaired neuroimmune axis. Inspired by how nerve cells metabolize glucose to generate the energy-carrying molecule adenosine triphosphate (ATP)27, NeuroAxis incorporates a glucose fuel cell (GFC) that oxidizes endogenous glucose to generate electrical energy for powering the entire system. Meanwhile, the glucose oxidation process also serves as metabolic interoceptive feedback to periodically infer metabolic states. The metabolic feedback is relayed to a logic circuit, which then autonomously regulates neuroeffector output through vagus nerve stimulation (VNS). The activation of this immunomodulatory circuit subsequently re-establishes metabolic homeostasis and ameliorates diabetes mellitus. Functionally, the GFC, logic circuit and morphing electrode recapitulate the afferent vagal nerve, brainstem and efferent vagal nerve, respectively, within the neuroimmune axis (Fig. 1a). In a type 2 diabetic rat model, the glucose-responsive NeuroAxis substantially improved glycaemic control, body weight regulation and immune–metabolic homeostasis. In a type 1 diabetic rat model, NeuroAxis alleviated the inflammatory immune response and enhanced β-cell activity, thereby facilitating the re-establishment of normal glycaemic homeostasis.

The bioinspired NeuroAxis consists of three core components: the GFC for metabolic feedback and energy input, a flexible printed circuit board (FPCB) for logic control and a soft morphing electrode for neural stimulation28 (Fig. 1b,c and Supplementary Fig. 1). At the system level, the self-regulating logic circuit continuously monitors glucose concentration through the terminal voltage of the GFC (Fig. 1d). The power management integrated circuit (PMIC) uses maximum power point tracking to optimize energy extraction from the GFC. Its integrated boost charger harvests and stores the energy in a capacitor. The on-chip buck converter provides a stable power supply for the microcontroller and peripherals when sufficient harvested power is available. Based on the glucose concentration, the logic circuit outputs a specific electrical stimulation pattern to the vagus nerve on the oesophagus through the morphing electrode. NeuroAxis was implanted subcutaneously into the rat abdominal region, with the GFC and FPCB placed into the abdominal subcutaneous space, while the morphing electrode was interfaced with the oesophageal vagus nerve (Fig. 1e).

Industry observers note that to realize the dual functions of sensing and powering, we designed a GFC in which the electrode was a porous, water-wicking carbon nanotube (CNT) electrode (Supplementary Fig. 2). The anode was decorated with Au nanoparticles (average diameter, 9.33 nm) on the CNT electrode (CNT-AuNP). These small-diameter Au nanoparticles exhibit glucose oxidase-like nanozyme activity, enabling catalytic oxidation of glucose to gluconate and generating an electrochemical current to power the control module29 (Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Fig. 3). At the cathode, a platinum-nanoparticle-coated CNT foam electrode (CNT-PtNP) can catalyse the reduction of oxygen and complete the redox cycle30,31. When immersed in glucose solution, CNT-AuNP and CNT-PtNP electrodes revealed distinct redox peaks, and the CNT-AuNP electrode generated a substantially larger current response to glucose than to the tested potential interferents (Fig. 2a–c and Supplementary Fig. 4). Both electrodes had b values (slope of log–log analysis of cyclic voltammetry) close to 0.5, indicating diffusion-controlled kinetics (Fig. 2d). Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy showed a reduced transfer resistance after AuNP and PtNP modification, suggesting enhanced interfacial electron transfer (Supplementary Fig. 5).

Sources indicate that across the physiological and pathological glucose range (3–30 mM), the power density of the GFC exhibited a nearly linear increase with glucose concentration (Fig. 2e,f). The open-circuit voltage also revealed a higher response to glucose than to the tested potential interferents (Fig. 2g and Supplementary Fig. 6). The large electrochemical surface area of the porous structure yielded higher power density and higher open-circuit voltage compared with that of non-porous structure (Extended Data Fig. 2). Enzyme-mediated GFCs are costly and unstable in vivo32,33, retaining only around 0.5% of baseline power density after 30 day immersion in glucose solution. By contrast, our nanozyme-based GFC retained 79.7% of baseline power density after 31 days in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) containing glucose and retained 64.5% of baseline power density after 90 days in PBS containing glucose and 1% bovine serum albumin (Fig. 2h, Extended Data Fig. 3 and Supplementary Fig. 7a). Moreover, accelerated ageing tests further indicated that the nanozyme-based GFC was estimated to retain approximately 50% of its initial power density after nearly 6 months (180 days) of incubation in PBS/glucose/bovine serum albumin solution (Supplementary Fig. 7b–e), indicating good stability of the nanozyme-based GFC.

To interface with the soft, deformable and dynamically moving oesophageal vagus nerve, we designed a low-impedance morphing electrode with a tissue-like Young’s modulus, high stretchability and intraoperative reconfigurability28 (Fig. 2i,j and Supplementary Fig. 8). The electrode comprises poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):poly(styrene sulfonate) (PEDOT:PSS)/glycerol as a conductive layer and poly(dimethylsiloxane)-isophorone bisurea (PDMS-IU) and PDMS-isophorone bisurea-4,4′-methylenebis(phenyl urea) (PDMS-IU-MPU) as encapsulation layers34 (Supplementary Fig. 9). Its robust self-healing property (Supplementary Fig. 10) allowed the device to transform from a two-dimensional (2D) film into an enclosed loop around the oesophagus. Owing to its non-Newtonian behaviour, the morphing electrode can form a seamless interface with target tissues without previous knowledge of their size and morphology. Moreover, the morphing electrode maintained stable electrical performance over 1,000 expansion cycles (Fig. 2k,l and Supplementary Video 1) and 8 weeks of soaking in PBS (Supplementary Fig. 11).

According to recent reports, the biocompatibility of NeuroAxis was further evaluated in vitro. After 7 days of incubation, cell viability was comparable to that of the control (Supplementary Figs. 12 and 13). Moreover, haemolysis tests revealed a low haemolysis ratio after 12 h of incubation with rat red blood cells (Supplementary Fig. 14).

It has been revealed that neuroAxis monitors interstitial glucose concentration and initiates neuromodulatory stimulation only under sustained hyperglycaemia35. Every 30 min, the GFC terminal voltage is sampled by NeuroAxis and can be converted to estimated blood glucose concentration through a voltage-to-glucose calibration curve (Fig. 3a, Supplementary Fig. 15 and Supplementary Video 2). We use a glucose level of 11.1 mM (corresponding to an input voltage of 0.6 V) as a threshold for hyperglycaemia in diabetic rats36,37. To avoid activation by transient postprandial glucose fluctuation in healthy animals, which typically return to baseline in 2 h, electrical stimulation is triggered only when glucose levels are consistently above the threshold for five consecutive readings (Fig. 3b). When triggered, the system delivers 3 min of biphasic VNS before returning to the sensing state (Fig. 3c,d and Supplementary Video 3). At a glucose concentration of 7 mM, which corresponds to normoglycaemia in healthy rats, the GFC can achieve a glucose-to-energy conversion efficiency of approximately 3.43% and generate sufficient power that exceeds the FPCB’s power consumption, enabling sustained, battery-less operation for NeuroAxis (Supplementary Figs. 16 and 17).

In a recent development, in vivo VNS elicited evoked compound action potentials with stereotyped waveforms after NeuroAxis implantation, which remained stable 1 month after implantation (amplitude of around 0.44 mV; Fig. 3e and Supplementary Figs. 18–20). Moreover, the evoked compound action potentials recorded from the cervical and abdominal vagus nerves, the increased FOS expression in the nodose ganglia and the elevated serum acetylcholine (ACh) levels collectively support that NeuroAxis stimulation simultaneously engages both the afferent and efferent vagal pathways (Supplementary Figs. 21 and 22). Open-field testing under stimulated and non-stimulated conditions highlighted comparable exploration without freezing, thigmotaxis or abnormal movements, and the total travel distance did not differ significantly between groups (Extended Data Fig. 4). Furthermore, X-ray and micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) confirmed stable placement and a conformal neural interface (Fig. 3f,g). NeuroAxis produced no measurable temperature increase during operation and caused no observable behavioural abnormalities, inflammatory responses or substantial alterations in serum biochemical and haematological parameters over 8 weeks of implantation (Fig. 3h,i, Extended Data Fig. 5 and Supplementary Figs. 23–25). Moreover, once the treatment was completed and the animals recovered to a stable condition, NeuroAxis could be readily explanted (Supplementary Fig. 26). These results suggest that NeuroAxis did not cause obvious adverse effects and was well tolerated in vivo.

Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is closely associated with insulin resistance, chronic obesity, low-grade inflammation and neuroendocrine dysfunction3,11. We first assessed the six-week therapeutic effects of NeuroAxis in an obesity-associated T2DM rat model12,13, assigning animals to four groups: healthy controls (group 1, G1); diabetic controls without implantation (G2); diabetic rats implanted with inactive NeuroAxis (G3); and diabetic rats implanted with a fully functional NeuroAxis (G4). Compared with rats in G2 and G3, rats in G4 showed sustained reductions in food intake and body weight (Fig. 4a,b), with visibly lower adiposity (Fig. 4c). Besides, blood glucose levels in G4 fell to near-healthy levels after treatment for 2 weeks, whereas hyperglycaemia persisted in G2 and G3 throughout the 6-week period (Fig. 4d,e). As further evidence of progressive glycaemic normalization, the GFC output voltage from NeuroAxis, which is closely associated with blood glucose concentration, gradually decreased in G4 during treatment (Extended Data Fig. 6).

Scale bars, 100 μm (m) and 5 cm (c).

Compared with G2 and G3, G4 had significantly lower fasting glucose and circulating insulin levels, resulting in lower Homeostatic Model Assessment of Insulin Resistance (HOMA-IR) scores (Fig. 4f–h). Intraperitoneal glucose tolerance tests (GTTs) and insulin tolerance tests (ITTs) further corroborated metabolic restoration. At week 6, G4 exhibited substantially faster glucose clearance and enhanced insulin responsiveness compared with G2 and G3, with decreased glycaemic excursions and reduced areas under the curve (AUCs) for glucose response (Fig. 4i–l). Importantly, although NeuroAxis entered standby mode as glycaemia was restored by week 2, the therapeutic benefits persisted beyond 6 weeks. Moreover, NeuroAxis treatment significantly reduced adipocyte hypertrophy in inguinal white adipose tissue (iWAT), epididymal white adipose tissue (eWAT) and interscapular brown adipose tissue (BAT), and alleviated the vacuole-like changes and hepatic lipid accumulation in the liver (Fig. 4m–p and Supplementary Fig. 27). Furthermore, immunohistochemical and immunofluorescence staining of pancreatic sections revealed enhanced insulin synthesis in G4 compared with G2, approaching the level observed in G1 (Extended Data Fig. 7). Collectively, our data suggest that NeuroAxis increases insulin sensitivity, normalizes glucose homeostasis, restores β-cell function and broadly mitigates metabolic dysfunction in obesity-associated T2DM with a persistent therapeutic effect.

It has been revealed that we also evaluated the long-term operational stability of NeuroAxis in vivo. In NeuroAxis-treated diabetic rats (G4), the proportion of operational devices after several weeks was mainly attributed to the normalization of blood glucose after effective treatment, together with the gradual reduction in GFC output. By contrast, because rats in the inactive NeuroAxis group (G3) remained hyperglycaemic throughout the study period, most devices in this group remained powered after long-term implantation for up to 90 days (Supplementary Fig. 28). Explanted G4 devices showed no obvious structural or circuit damage and could effectively deliver electrical stimulation output when exposed to higher glucose concentrations after 90 days of implantation (Supplementary Fig. 29). These results suggest that the NeuroAxis can operate effectively under hyperglycaemic conditions after 3 months of implantation. Longer-term applications will require further improvements in biofuel cell stability and adaptive threshold setting.

According to recent reports, recent advances in neuroimmunology have revealed that stimulation of the vagus nerve triggers the release of ACh, which binds to α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (α7nAChR) expressed on immune cells. The cholinergic signalling pathway can suppress obesity-associated inflammation by inhibiting the production of proinflammatory cytokines9,12,38,39. We therefore hypothesize that NeuroAxis can ameliorate T2DM by engaging α7nAChR signalling. To test our hypothesis, we included a fifth cohort (G5): diabetic rats implanted with an active NeuroAxis and given methyllycaconitine citrate (MLA), a selective α7nAChR antagonist, to pharmacologically block cholinergic anti-inflammatory signalling40,41 (Fig. 5a). G5 exhibited substantially poorer glycaemic control compared with G4, supporting the role of the cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway in mediating the therapeutic benefit of NeuroAxis (Supplementary Fig. 30).
