To investigate NeuroAxis-mediated immunoregulation, we evaluated the concentration of inflammatory cytokines and the infiltration of macrophages in adipose tissues. ACh levels were elevated in both G4 and G5, supporting the activation of the cholinergic pathway during NeuroAxis stimulation (Fig. 5b). However, only G4 had increased concentrations of the anti-inflammatory cytokine interleukin-10 (IL-10) in adipose tissues and decreased concentrations of the proinflammatory cytokines interleukin-1β (IL-1β) and tumour necrosis factor (TNF) in adipose tissues and serum (Fig. 5c–e and Supplementary Fig. 31). By contrast, the cytokine levels in G5 were comparable to G2, with a negligible immunoregulatory effect. Moreover, the flow cytometry analysis suggested that G4 had lower total macrophage infiltration and proinflammatory macrophage (M1-like macrophage) infiltration, and higher anti-inflammatory macrophage (M2-like macrophage) infiltration, compared with G2. Furthermore, the infiltration of lipid-associated macrophages was reduced only in G4 and not in G5 (Fig. 5f–j and Supplementary Fig. 32). Moreover, G5 had lower CD163 expression and higher CD86 expression in adipose tissue compared with G4 (Fig. 5k–m). The time-course analysis of macrophage phenotypes and inflammatory cytokines revealed that active NeuroAxis treatment induced an early shift from pro-inflammatory to anti-inflammatory macrophage profiles, accompanied by reduced local and systemic TNF and IL-1β levels from day 7 to day 21 (Supplementary Fig. 33). These effects were not observed in G2, G3 and G5, supporting the involvement of α7nAChR-mediated cholinergic signalling in inflammatory attenuation. These results suggest that inflammatory attenuation occurs early during NeuroAxis treatment and may contribute to the subsequent metabolic improvements. Furthermore, NeuroAxis treatment (G4) improved glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity in diabetic rats, as shown by reduced blood glucose excursions and lower AUC in both the GTT and ITT compared with G2 and G3 (Supplementary Fig. 34). These beneficial effects were substantially attenuated by MLA administration (G5), supporting the involvement of α7nAChR-mediated cholinergic signalling in NeuroAxis-induced metabolic regulation.

We next investigated the relative contributions of vagal afferent and efferent pathways to the therapeutic effects of NeuroAxis. NeuroAxis stimulation activates afferent vagal pathway projecting to central metabolic circuits, as evidenced by increased FOS expression in the hypothalamic regions involved in feeding regulation42 (Supplementary Fig. 35). Consistently, NeuroAxis-mediated VNS increased circulating concentrations of the satiety- and glucose-regulatory hormones cholecystokinin octapeptide-8 (CCK-8) and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), whereas vagotomy attenuated these effects, suggesting that these hormonal responses depend on intact vagal–brainstem connectivity42 (Supplementary Fig. 36). These results suggest that NeuroAxis engages a vagal afferent–brainstem axis to reduce food intake and regulate body weight. However, reduced food intake and body weight loss alone do not fully explain the metabolic benefits of NeuroAxis, because pair-feeding resulted in only modest improvements in glucose control (Supplementary Fig. 37). Moreover, NeuroAxis-treated rats that underwent vagotomy maintained better glycaemic control than those treated with MLA, despite showing less body weight reduction (Extended Data Fig. 8). These findings suggest that, relative to the vagal afferent pathway, the efferent α7nAChR-mediated cholinergic pathway is likely to be more closely linked to inflammation suppression, improved insulin sensitivity and improved glycaemic control. Moreover, metabolic cage analyses further indicated that NeuroAxis treatment restored the average respiratory exchange ratio towards healthy control levels, suggesting improved glucose utilization and metabolic flexibility in G4 rats43 (Supplementary Fig. 38). Collectively, vagal afferent signalling primarily regulates feeding and body weight, whereas α7nAChR-mediated cholinergic signalling mainly attenuates inflammation and promotes insulin sensitivity and glucose homeostasis.

In a recent development, to further assess the therapeutic effect on systemic metabolic dysfunction, we performed integrated transcriptomic–metabolomic profiling of liver tissue after 6 weeks of NeuroAxis treatment in T2DM rats. We observed broad reprogramming of hepatocellular functions in response to NeuroAxis therapy. Specifically, NeuroAxis treatment was associated with coordinated downregulation of pro-inflammatory genes (such as Nfkb1, Tnf, Il1b and Il6) and upregulation of insulin-signalling-related genes (such as Insr, Irs1, Pik3ca and Akt1). Consistent with these transcriptional changes, metabolomic analysis revealed alterations in glucose metabolism and mitochondrial function, including changes in glucose-6-phosphate, lactate, citrate and other tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle intermediates44. Circulating 1,5-anhydroglucitol, a marker inversely correlated with glucosuria due to reduced renal reabsorption, also increased after NeuroAxis stimulation, suggesting an overall improvement in glycaemic control45. Lipidomic profiling further revealed a shift from saturated and monohydroxy fatty acids (FAs) toward monounsaturated and polyunsaturated FAs. This shift is generally indicative of enhanced lipid use and potentially reduced lipotoxic stress13,46. Moreover, bile acid turnover and vitamin metabolism were modulated in the NeuroAxis group, consistent with partial restoration of hepatic metabolic homeostasis47. The integrated pathway mapping suggested that NeuroAxis treatment alleviates systemic chronic inflammation, restores PI3K–AKT pathway function to improve glucose uptake and metabolism, and promotes hepatic glycogenesis and mitochondrial activity, both of which are downstream targets of vagus nerve-mediated anti-inflammatory circuits12,48,49 (Fig. 5n,o and Extended Data Fig. 9a–e). These molecular reprogramming events are accompanied by systemic improvements in metabolic and inflammatory status in the NeuroAxis-treated group (G4), as evidenced by reduced circulating TNF, IL-1β, leptin, cholesterol, triglycerides and haemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), alongside increased levels of ghrelin and adiponectin (Extended Data Fig. 9f–m).

Sources indicate that importantly, comparison between G4 and G5 further showed that pharmacological blockade of α7nAChR with MLA attenuated NeuroAxis-induced metabolic and transcriptional remodelling. Compared with G4, G5 showed reactivation of inflammation-associated metabolic reprogramming and hepatic insulin resistance, characterized by elevated TCA cycle, glycolytic and branched-chain amino acids metabolites, increased NF-κB related pro-inflammatory and gluconeogenic gene expression, and reduced anti-inflammatory and insulin signalling markers (Supplementary Fig. 39). Additional transcriptomic comparisons further showed that G4 was transcriptionally close to the healthy control group (G1), with no prominent enrichment of diabetes-associated inflammatory or metabolic dysfunction pathways. By contrast, the differences between G4 and the inactive NeuroAxis group (G3) largely resembled those observed between G4 and diabetic rats (G2), involving inflammatory response, insulin resistance, NF-κB signalling, FA metabolism and related metabolic pathways (Supplementary Fig. 40). Collectively, all of the results highlight that NeuroAxis restores the function of the neuroimmune axis, thereby alleviating systemic chronic inflammation, enhancing insulin signalling and promoting glucose and lipid homeostasis, ultimately reprogramming hepatic metabolism to support metabolic recovery in T2DM rats.

To demonstrate NeuroAxis as a general approach for treating metabolic diseases, we further evaluated the therapeutic potential of NeuroAxis for type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM), which is primarily driven by dysregulated immune response10,50. Animals were divided into four groups (G1–4), similar to the experiments in T2DM rats. Compared with G2 and G3, G4 highlighted improved glycaemic control as reflected by reduced blood glucose and HbA1c levels and elevated circulating insulin (Fig. 6a–c). Normal glycaemic control was achieved by week 8 for G4.

NeuroAxis treatment attenuated inflammatory immune cell infiltration and activation associated with β-cell attack. It increased regulatory T (Treg) cells while reducing CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in both spleen and pancreas, promoted M2-like macrophage infiltration in the pancreas and decreased CD45RA+ B cells and antigen-presenting dendritic cells (DCs) in the spleen (Fig. 6d–f and Extended Data Fig. 10). These changes were accompanied by elevated anti-inflammatory cytokines (TGF-β and IL-10) in the pancreas and reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF, IFNγ, IL-2 and IL-1β) in the pancreas and blood, together with lower pancreatic CD8 and CD86 expression (Fig. 6g,h and Supplementary Fig. 41), indicating suppressed inflammatory immune responses in the pancreatic microenvironment.

Moreover, representative immunofluorescence images showed direct evidence of increased BrdU+ β cells and restored β-cell mass in the pancreas in G4 compared with in G2 and G3. These data suggest that the proliferative activity of β cells is enhanced after NeuroAxis treatment (Fig. 6i,j), consistent with previous studies supporting a role for vagal nerve signalling in the regulation of β-cell proliferation6,51,52. Time-course insulin staining over a broader pancreatic area further showed that NeuroAxis treatment (G4) progressively restored insulin-positive β-cell mass in diabetic rats, with detectable improvement after 2 weeks and a substantial increase after 8 weeks compared with diabetic (G2) and inactive NeuroAxis controls (G3) (Supplementary Fig. 42). Consistently, histological analysis by haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining demonstrated improved islet structural integrity and cellular organization in G4 (Fig. 6k). The GTT results further showed that G4 exhibited a metabolic profile close to healthy controls (G1) (Fig. 6l,m). Together, these results indicate that NeuroAxis reshapes the streptozotocin-induced inflammatory pancreatic microenvironment, suppresses immune-cell infiltration and activation, and promotes β-cell proliferative recovery, thereby restoring glycaemic control.

By mimicking energy metabolism and signal transduction in biological systems, we conceived a fully autonomous artificial neuroimmune axis that harvests energy from endogenous glucose while transducing metabolic cues into vagal output. In contrast to existing vagus nerve stimulators4,20, NeuroAxis directly couples real-time fluctuations in blood glucose to self-regulated vagal stimulation, restoring the cholinergic anti-inflammatory reflex. The GFC simultaneously harvests metabolic energy and senses biochemical signals, enabling chemically responsive neuromodulation without battery or wireless power transfer.

By functionally recapitulating the autonomic interoceptive system, NeuroAxis exerts systemic effects on peripheral targets, including attenuating chronic inflammation, reducing inflammatory immune response, enhancing pancreatic β-cell activity and insulin sensitivity, normalizing glycaemic control and, ultimately, reestablishing metabolic and immune homeostasis. NeuroAxis remained functional under hyperglycaemic conditions after 3 months of implantation in rats, although further optimization of the GFC will be required to improve long-term operational stability for translational applications. By restoring the impaired neuroimmune axis, NeuroAxis provides a complementary strategy to conventional pharmacotherapies and opens a path towards personalized, metabolism-driven neuromodulation for immunometabolic disorders. More broadly, this intelligent bioelectronic system establishes a general framework for engineering artificial interoceptive circuits that restore interorgan communication and treat complex multisystem diseases.

Recent findings suggest that for preparation of porous electrode, the carboxylated multiwalled CNTs (MWCNT-COOH, XFNANO, 0.6 g), graphite (Sigma-Aldrich, 0.1 g) and NaHCO3 (Sigma-Aldrich, 6.0 g) were completely mixed, and then SEBS was added (Asahi Kasei Tuftec H1062, 30 wt% in toluene, 8 g) and the mixture was stirred at 3,000 rpm for 5 min (ref. 53). Then, 3 ml toluene was added, stirred at 3,000 rpm for 5 min, poured into a rectangular mould (1 mm thickness), transferred into ethanol solution for solvent exchange and finally dried under ambient conditions overnight. After drying, the electrode was soaked in 0.5 M HCl for 6 h to completely remove NaHCO3, washed with distilled water and then dried in an oven at 80 °C overnight to form porous flexible CNT electrode. The CNT electrode was cut into 2 cm2 (1 cm × 2 cm) size. For the fabrication of the anode, the CNT electrode was immersed in HAuCl4 (Sigma-Aldrich, 1 mM) and PVP (Sigma-Aldrich, 4 mg ml−1) mixture for 30 min, and then NaBH4 (Sigma-Aldrich, 10 mM) was added for 30 min to grow Au nanoparticles on the surface of the CNT electrode (CNT-AuNP electrode). For the fabrication of the cathode, the CNT electrode was immersed in H2PtCl6 (Sigma-Aldrich, 0.1 mg ml−1) solution, and then NaBH4 (10 mM) was added gradually under 80 °C for 1 h to grow Pt nanoparticles on the CNT electrode (CNT-PtNP electrode). Nafion 117 solution (Sigma-Aldrich) was drop-cast on the CNT-Pt electrode and allowed to dry to enhance proton transport within the electrode. The morphologies of the anode and cathode were characterized by SEM (Hitachi Regulus 8230). For electrochemical measurements, the Ag/AgCl electrode and platinum wire were used as reference and counter electrode, respectively. The cyclic voltammetry, chronoamperometry, polarization curves, impedance spectroscopy and open-circuit voltage of the electrode and GFC were tested in PBS with different concentrations of glucose at room temperature.

Sources indicate that the fabrication of the morphing electrode followed our previous works28. In brief, the self-healing viscoelastic polymer (VP) were prepared by mixing PDMS-IU with a PDMS-IU0.4-MPU0.6 in toluene (20 wt%) under a weight ratio of 1:3. The PEDOT:PSS/glycerol mixture was prepared by mixed PEDOT:PSS (Orgacon ICP 1050, Agfa) and glycerol with a dry weight ratio of 1:32, and then filtered through a 0.45-μm syringe filter. The glass substrate was first treated by oxygen plasma (Technics Micro-RIE Series 800) at 150 W for 45 s, spin-coated with PEDOT:PSS/glycerol mixture at a speed of 400 rpm for 1 min, followed by drying at room temperature for 8 h to form PEDOT:PSS/glycerol film. After electronic design by using AutoCAD software, the PEDOT:PSS/glycerol film on glass substrate was laser-engraved by an ultraviolet laser cutter with 1.0 W cm−2 power (Protolaser U4, LPKF). The VP (20 wt% toluene) was preheated at 70 °C, drop cast on the PEDOT:PSS/glycerol pattern, dried under ambient conditions overnight and then heated in oven at 70 °C for 2 h to enhance the attachment of VP with PEDOT:PSS/glycerol film. The size and thickness of PEDOT:PSS/glycerol film and VP were measured by using an optical microscope (Keyence, VK-X3000). The morphology of electrode was characterized by using SEM (Hitachi Regulus 8230). The electrical and electrochemical performance of morphing electrode was characterized by using electrochemical workstation (PalmSens4). The mechanical properties of the morphing electrode were characterized by using a tensile testing system (Instron, 5565).

The circuit integrates a BLE module (BC840, Fanstel), an energy harvester/power management integrated circuit (BQ25570, TI), two low-power digital-to-analogue converters (DACs) (MCP4725, Microchip Technology) and supporting passive components. The BC840 module, based on the Nordic nRF52840 system-on-chip (SoC), integrates a 64 MHz, 32 bit Arm Cortex M4F MCU, a 2.4 GHz multiprotocol transceiver, and an integrated PCB trace antenna, enabling compact wireless operation. It acquires GFC signals through its built-in successive approximation analogue-to-digital converter (SAADC) and transmits data to a smartphone through BLE, with the SAADC shut down when idle to reduce power consumption. The BQ25570 harvests energy from the GFC, boosts the input voltage and stores the harvested energy in a capacitor, then provides a regulated power supply for the whole system. Two MCP4725 DACs generate a 10 Hz biphasic stimulation waveform (0.5 ms pulse width, ±2 V amplitude) for stimulation. Both DACs communicate through I2C and support power-down mode which can be controlled by the BC840. The FPCB was fabricated by JLCPCB using EasyEDA design tools and encapsulated in a silicone shell for better biocompatibility and water resistance (Supplementary Fig. 43 and Supplementary Table 1).

The FPCB was first coated with parylene C (30 µm) by using a Parylene coater (SCS Coatings, Labcoater3) and the contact pads were then exposed by laser ablation. The polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS, Dow Corning) was further dipped in FPCB for mechanical encapsulation of the joints between FPCB and GFC, then cured at 75 °C for 20 min to form the PDMS encapsulation layer. The medical grade silicone elastomer (Avantor) was fabricated by using 3D printer (Lynxter S300X) and further using to encapsulate the FPCB by using Kwik-Sil glue (World Precision Instruments). After encapsulation with silicone elastomer, all devices were further coated with parylene C (10 μm) by using Parylene coater. For GFC assembly, the connection points of FPCB were exposed, and then connected with CNT-AuNP and CNT-PtNP by using silver paste (Dycotec Materials) and curing at 80 °C for 1 h. After that, both the anode and cathode were dipped with alginate (2% in H2O, 200 μl, Sigma-Aldrich) solution, and then immerse to calcium chloride (1 mM, Sigma-Aldrich) solution for 30 min to fabricate an alginate hydrogel layer on the surface of the electrode to enhance the biocompatibility of the GFC.

Recent findings suggest that the glucose-responsive logic control of NeuroAxis received input from periodic sampling terminal voltage of GFC, which can represent glucose concentration. The output of the GFC was directly connected to the input of SAADC port of BC840 and power-harvest module. Specifically, the terminal voltage of the GFC was sampled once every 30 min. When the detected voltage exceeded 0.6 V, the high-voltage count was incremented; otherwise, the counter was reset to zero. Once the high-voltage count reached five, the system output electrical stimulation for 3 min. As the output voltage of the GFC exhibits a linear correlation with glucose concentration, the terminal voltage of GFC can be directly used to estimate blood glucose levels. This strategy ensured that stimulation was selectively initiated under sustained hyperglycaemic conditions, thereby reducing the likelihood of false triggering caused by transient voltage fluctuations. To experimentally evaluate the logical control function, the GFC was immersed in glucose solutions of varying concentrations. During the testing, the sampling interval was set to 10 s. The terminal voltage of the GFC was continuously acquired and transmitted to cell phones through a BC840 BLE module, while the corresponding output signals of NeuroAxis were simultaneously recorded using an oscilloscope.

In a recent development, all animal experiments were conducted in strict accordance with the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of the National University of Singapore (2024-0090) and Nanjing University (SYXK2024-0067). Rats were housed under controlled environmental conditions (22 °C, 60–70% humidity) under a 12 h–12 h light–dark cycle. To establish an obesity-induced T2DM rat model, male Sprague-Dawley rats (aged 8 weeks) were fed a high-fat diet (60% kcal from fat; D12492, Research Diets) for 6 weeks. Subsequently, diabetes was induced by a single intraperitoneal injection of streptozotocin (STZ, 35 mg per kg body weight) dissolved in 0.1 M sodium citrate buffer. Blood glucose levels were monitored daily for 2 weeks after injection13. Before the initiation of treatment, G2–G7 rats were switched to a standard chow diet and maintained on this diet throughout the experimental period. This design allowed us to evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of NeuroAxis-mediated stimulation without the confounding influence of continued high-fat diet feeding. To establish a T1DM rat model, male Sprague-Dawley rats (aged 8 weeks) received intraperitoneal injections of STZ (50 mg per kg) dissolved in ice-cold 0.1 M citrate buffer (pH 4.5) for five consecutive days to induce a multiple-low-dose STZ-induced T1DM rat model50. Rats exhibiting sustained hyperglycaemia (blood glucose > 11.1 mM) were considered to be diabetic and selected for device implantation procedures6,50. Rats were divided into seven groups: healthy controls (G1), diabetic controls without implantation (G2), diabetic rats implanted with inactive NeuroAxis, which cut off the connection between the FPCB and the morphing electrode (G3), diabetic rats implanted with a fully functional NeuroAxis (G4), diabetic rats implanted with a fully functional NeuroAxis plus MLA (intraperitoneal injection, 5 mg kg−1, once every 2 days) (G5), diabetic rats with a fully functional NeuroAxis with and vagotomy (ligated by using a 4-0 silk suture) above the implanted electrode (G6), diabetic rats implanted with a fully functional NeuroAxis, vagotomy and MLA administration (G7). MLA administration and vagotomy were used to block the anti-inflammatory pathway and ascending vagal signalling, respectively. To minimize variability associated with circadian rhythms and measurement timing, body weight, non-fasting blood glucose and food intake were measured between 10:00 and 11:00 for all animals.

It has been revealed that after implantation with devices for 6 weeks, the rats were anaesthetized using isoflurane inhalation (3% for induction, 1.5–2% for maintenance) with oxygen supplementation, and CT imaging was captured using microPET/CT imaging system (Hiscan) under the following conditions: 80 kV scanning tube voltage, 100 μA scanning tube current, 25 µm focal spot and a 50 ms exposure time. The images were reconstructed into three-dimensional images by using Hiscan VM Pro software (Hiscan).

Recent findings suggest that for GTTs and ITTs, all rats were fasted for 6–7 h. After intraperitoneal glucose injection (1 g kg−1 body weight), blood glucose levels were monitored from the tail vein after (0, 15, 30, 60, 90 and 120 min) using a glucometer for GTTs. For ITTs, rats were injected with 0.5 U kg−1 body weight insulin intraperitoneally and glucose levels were assessed over time (0, 15, 30, 60, 90 and 120 min). The insulin resistance was calculated by HOMA-IR, defined as fasting glucose (mmol l−1) × fasting insulin (µU ml−1)/22.5 (ref. 54).

Sources indicate that the spleen, adipose tissues and pancreas were collected from rats, finely minced and subjected to enzymatic digestion in a collagenase IV solution (1× HBSS supplemented with 10 mM HEPES (Sigma-Aldrich), 1.5 mg ml−1 collagenase IV (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and 8.25 µg ml−1 DNase I (Sigma-Aldrich)) at 37 °C for 30 min. The cell suspension was then passed through a 70-µm nylon mesh filter (Corning) to remove tissue debris, followed by red blood cell lysis using Red Cell Lysis Buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). After lysis, cell suspensions were centrifuged at 750 rpm for 3 min and the supernatant was removed. Cells were stained with fluorescence-labelled antibodies CD45 (BioLegend, 202220 and 202225, 1:200), CD11b (BioLegend, 201805, 1:200), CD11c (BioLegend, 201819, 1:200), MHC-II (BioLegend, 205405, 1:200), CD80 (BioLegend, 200205, 1:200), CD68 (BioLegend, 201003 and 137007, 1:200), CD86 (BioLegend, 200315, 1:200), CD163 (Abcam, ab313666, 1:500), CD3 (BioLegend, 201403, 1:200), CD4 (BioLegend, 201507, 1:200), CD8 (BioLegend, 201715, 1:200), CD25 (BioLegend, 202115, 1:200), FOXP3 (BioLegend, 320013, 1:200), CD9 (BioLegend, 206505, 1:200) and TREM2 (BioLegend, 824805, 1:200), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Cells were sorted on the SA3800 (Sony) sorter and analysed in FlowJo.

In a recent development, after slicing, the tissue sections were rapidly frozen and then sectioned using a cryotome. The sections were further incubated with the primary antibodies, including anti-CD86 antibody (Abcam, ab238468, 1:500), anti-CD163 antibody (Abcam, ab182422, 1:500), anti-CD8 antibody (Abcam, ab237709, 1:500), anti-FOS antibody (Abcam, ab302667, 1:500), anti-insulin antibody (Abcam, ab181547, 1:500) and anti-BrdU antibody (Abcam, ab6326, 1:500) at room temperature for 2 h. For BrdU staining, rats were administered with BrdU (BD Bioscience) diluted in drinking water (0.8 mg ml−1). The sections were then incubated with fluorescein (FITC)-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 111-095-003, 1:500), FITC-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 115-095-062, 1:500), tetramethylrhodamine isothiocyanate (TRITC)-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 115-025-062, 1:500) for 1 h, and finally stained with 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) for 30 min and imaged using a digital pathological section scanner (Olympus VS200). For β-cell mass quantification, total pancreatic and insulin-positive areas of each section were measured by using Olympus OlyVIA software (Olympus). The β-cell mass was finally calculated as the average insulin-positive area relative to the total pancreatic area, multiplied by the pancreatic weight.

Industry observers note that rat liver tissues were collected 6 weeks after implantation. After washing three times with PBS, approximately 30 mg of each sample was placed into a 2 ml microcentrifuge tube containing 200 μl of prechilled water and two stainless-steel beads. The tissues were homogenized twice at 55 Hz for 60 s each using a tissue grinder. Subsequently, 800 μl of methanol:chloroform (1:1, v/v) was added, and the mixture was sonicated for 30 min in an ultrasonic bath. Samples were incubated at −20 °C for 45 min to precipitate proteins, followed by centrifugation at 12,000 rpm and 4 °C for 20 min. The resulting supernatant (800 μl) was collected and dried under vacuum. The residues were reconstituted in 150 μl of 50% methanol containing 5 ppm 2-chloro-l-phenylalanine (internal standard) and vortexed for 30 s. After centrifugation at 12,000 rpm and 4 °C for 10 min, the solutions were filtered through 0.22-μm membranes and centrifuged again under the same conditions. The final supernatants were transferred into vials for analysis. To monitor instrument stability and data reproducibility, 10–20 μl of each supernatant was pooled to generate a quality control sample. All metabolomics experiments were conducted by Shanghai Personal Biotechnology.

In a recent development, for transcriptomic profiling, tissues were rinsed with RNase-free water to minimize contamination. Total RNA was extracted using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen) or a commercial RNA isolation kit, according to the manufacturer’s instructions. RNA quality and integrity were assessed with a NanoDrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies). Samples with RNA integrity number (RIN) ≥ 7.0 were considered to be suitable for further analysis. Library construction and sequencing were performed by Shanghai Personal Biotechnology. In brief, mRNA was enriched from total RNA using oligo (dT) magnetic beads, fragmented, and reverse-transcribed into cDNA. The resulting cDNA was end-repaired, A-tailed, adapter-ligated and PCR-amplified to generate sequencing libraries. Paired-end sequencing was conducted on an Illumina, producing high-quality reads for downstream analysis. Clean reads were aligned to the reference genome using the STAR aligner. Gene expression was quantified with HTSeq. Differentially expressed genes between groups were identified using DESeq2 with thresholds of |log2[fold change]| ≥ 1 and adjusted P < 0.05. Functional enrichment of differentially expressed genes was performed on the Personal Genes Cloud (https://www.genescloud.cn), based on the Gene Ontology (http://www.geneontology.org) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (http://www.genome.jp/kegg/) databases. Pathways with adjusted P < 0.05 were considered to be statistically significant.

Sources indicate that all experiments were conducted independently at least in triplicate. Data are presented as mean values with s.d. Comparisons within and between groups were assessed using unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-tests or one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s multiple-comparison post hoc test when appropriate. Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism software. P < 0.05 was considered to be statistically significant.

Recent findings suggest that logic control of NeuroAxis during closed-loop glucose-responsive neuromodulation. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The second international break of the season is upon us, which is a good time to take stock of how things are going beyond he men’s first team.

According to recent reports, an ownership and management should not just be judged on one area of the club, but rather multiple different departments. The youth sector needs to be developing players in the right way, while the rising prevalence of women’s football gives added impetus to make the Femminile side as competitive as possible.

It has been revealed that read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

In a recent development, that being stated, can be hard enough keeping up with how the senior team are doing without thinking about the various other sides operating under the Milan umbrella. So, we have provided a summary of how Milan Futuro, Milan Primavera and Milan Women are doing so far in 2026-27.

According to recent reports, it was all change over the summer for the Futuro as they brought in Sergio Navarro as the head coach. The idea was to create some continuity with Ruben Amorim’s more continental style of football, and the pedigree that the Spaniard has suggested it was a positive move.

While not a necessity, the objective for the campaign will no doubt have been set as competing for promotion back to the third tier, which is the level that the project started at prior to the relegation in 2024-25.

In a recent development, position: It is a case of so far, so good for Navarro’s men. They sit fourth in the standings with 23 points from 11 games, obtained through seven wins, two draws and two losses. They have scored 21 goals (third-most in the league) and allowed 15.

Importantly, the Futuro have a game in hand on the sides above them. If they win it they would go level with Chievo Verona (yes, that Chievo) and Nibbiano & Valtidone who are on 26 points. The former, however, have a 10 better goal difference.

The U23s are part of the Premier League International Cup and they got past Everton 2-1 in the first game, with matches against Stoke later this month and Tottenham in November to come, both away from home.

High point: On October 18, Milan’s second team went to the current league-leaders Chievo and beat them 2-1, with Bonomi scoring a late winner. That was an early marker of what this team are capable of. A special mention must go to the Premier League Cup win at Goodison Park against Everton, too.

Sources indicate that low point: That aforementioned win in Verona came in the round after Milan had lost 2-1 at home to Rovato Vertovese. They are a side that have only won twice all season and presently occupy the relegation spots, so it was a significant blow before a big response.

Recent findings suggest that key players: There have been multiple players that have stood out. Levin Asanji has scored four goals in the league, as has Lorenzo Ossolo. Fabio Pandolfi has been playing a deeper midfield role and looks to have quality well beyond his 18 years of age, with three goals to his name.

Silvano Vos is having a resurgence, while the likes of Emanuele Sala, Mattia Cappelletti, Alessandro Bonomi and Emanuele Borsani have all started every single game, aiding their development under the new coach. El Hadji Malick Cisse – a January arrival – is also turning a lot of heads.

For a bit more deeper reading on the tactical approach used by Milan Futuro under Navarro, we suggest reading the analysis we put out over the international break.

The 2025-26 season was a mixed one for the Primavera side, as their record of 11 wins and 11 defeats in 38 games highlights perfectly. They finished 11th, nine points off the relegation play-offs but 10 points off the Scudetto play-offs, though a lot of the younger talents had been again accelerated into the Futuro side.

Giovanni Renna remained at the helm going into the new campaign, the coach that has been promoted up the ranks and thus knows a lot of the players. The hope was that continuity would yield better results, and so far it has.

Industry observers note that position: At the time of writing, the U20 side are sixth in the Primavera 1 league, which puts them in a final play-off spot. They have won five of their first 10 games but they have also lost four, so they remain a bit of a rollercoaster ride of inconsistency.

Looking upwards, Parma are right now top on 21 points, but the Rossoneri are within striking distance of Inter, who are in second on 19 points. However, Renna’s side are also a bad round away from being in the bottom half too.

It has been revealed that milan Primavera progressed in the Coppa Italia Primavera at the end of October, beating Catanzaro 2-1 thanks to a late winner from Dotta. Como are the opponents in the next round.

According to recent reports, high point: It’s hard to look past the last two rounds in truth. The Primavera seem to have really clicked, scoring 10 goals in the last 180 minutes of action, beating Monza 5-0 away from home and then AlbinoLeffe 5-1 at home.

An honourable mention must go to the 2-0 win over Juventus in September, given they are in a similar position with also having a B-team (Juve Next Gen), so they will continue to serve as a useful point of comparison.

Industry observers note that low point: Back on October 10, the young Diavoli lost 2-0 against Atalanta which was their third league defeat in a row. There was talk of crisis mode as the slide down the table continued, and against an Atalanta side that are now third-bottom of the league. Thankfully, they turned it around swiftly.

Industry observers note that key players: A bit like with the Futuro, the goals have been shared around the Milan Primavera squad. Mattia Zaramella has emerged recently as a star with four goals, as has Max Anastasio who arrived from Bologna and has the same amount.

Industry observers note that then, Andrea Cullotta (a centre-back), Vincent Ibrahimovic (a midfielder) and Edoardo Tartaglia (a full-back) all have two goals. Renna has called upon the same core group of players largely. Matteo Geroli, Francesco Domnitei, Cullotta, Zaramella, Tartaglia, Anastasio and Yanis Massaouadi have all appeared in every round.

According to recent reports, last season was not one that Milan Women will want to shout about, given that they finished sixth in the table and seven points off the play-off spots in the end. They won just nine of 22 games, placing them below even Fiorentina and Lazio, plus Juventus, city rivals Inter and eventual champions Roma.

Recent findings suggest that however, like with the Primavera, consistency was the name of the game. So, Suzanne Bakker remained as the head coach, and there wasn’t as much player turnover as in some recent years.

Position: There have only been seven rounds so far in Serie A Femminile, but the Rossonere have got off to a stuttering start. They have just seven points from their opening seven games, which puts them in eighth place in the table. They have scored 11 goals but let in a joint-league-high 16.

Looking upwards, Roma lead the way with 21 points having won every game. Inter are second on 16 points – so nine more than Milan – while Juventus occupy the final play-off spot on 12. Over their shoulders, Sassuolo are in bottom (the only relegation spot), with three points.

In the Women’s Cup, Milan drew 1-1 with Como, beat Como 1907 (affiliated with the men’s team presently in Serie A, the others are a stand-alone club) 2-1, and then lost 1-0 to Juventus to end their campaign.

Recent findings suggest that high point: This one is quite an easy pick, and it has to be the 2-1 victory over Juventus last month. Thea Kyvåg and Monica Renzotti overturned Lenzini’s opener, which had come with just under a quarter of an hour left on the clock, engineering a late comeback that sparked jubilant scenes.

Low point: The tone for what has been a disappointing campaign so far for Bakker’s ladies was set in round one, when they were beaten 4-1 by Como 1907. Then, losing 1-0 away at Como was another dark day, given they have only won twice.

On November 7, the 3-0 derby defeat to Inter – which included a red card for Milan – served only to highlight the substantial gulf between the two teams at the moment.

Industry observers note that key players: Christy Grimshaw remains the shining light for Milan Women, with three goals and an assist to her name. The scoring charts then see Sara Stokic on three goals, with Sara Fornes, Park Soojeong and Monica Renzotti all netting twice.

Sources indicate that grimshaw is one of three players to start every game so far under Bakker, with the others being defenders Angelica Soffia and Nerea Nevado. Sandra Estevez has emerged as the number one between the sticks too.

Arsenal are alert to drones flying over the club’s training ground after footage of Mauricio Pochettino’s first session at Manchester United was captured.

The drone operator involved in that incident at Carrington has since apologised, but not before 12 minutes of the training session was filmed and then uploaded publicly on YouTube.

The United players and staff were clearly visible, as was the shape they were working on ahead of their trip to face Liverpool this weekend.

Arsenal have had a run-in with a drone themselves this season, when their Carabao Cup clash with Fleetwood last month was delayed for eight minutes as the authorities worked to locate the operator.

Asked about the latest incident at United, Arteta said: “Well, very delicate, obviously.

Sources indicate that “We had an episode as well against Fleetwood; you see what is happening around the world as well. So I don’t know what the solution is.

In a recent development, “Obviously, the technology is growing, the ability to get into systems is growing at a really rapid rate. We need to be very aware of that, but I cannot tell you what the solution is to that.”.

Clubs regularly use their own drones to film training sessions and later review footage.

Arteta confirmed that Arsenal have people in place to ensure there are no outside sources watching their sessions and that the team are protected, but he emphasised that was well beyond his list of responsibilities.

“They are looking after that constantly just in case it happens, but obviously what happened yesterday [at United], it’s a very serious matter,” Arteta said.

According to recent reports, “As I noted, I’m not a specialist, I don’t have a solution, I don’t have a clue. We have people that are in charge of that.

“There are authorities there now to try to prevent that, and that’s the only thing that we can do. Collaborate with them and try to avoid it.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Moscow has increasingly relied on a so-called shadow fleet to bypass Western sanctions and transport its oil around the world.

Other heavily sanctioned countries, including Iran and Venezuela, have also been accused of using such vessels to export petroleum products.

These tankers often rely on deceptive practices like turning off their location transponders to evade detection and conceal the cargo's true origins or destinations.

The fleet, which consists largely of aging, uninsured and poorly maintained tankers, has raised widespread concern across the shipping industry. Yet it has expanded rapidly in recent years and now accounts for nearly 19% of global oil tanker capacity, according to estimates by financial intelligence firm S&P Global.

"The shadow fleet is a scourge," Elisabeth Braw, senior fellow at the think tank Atlantic Council, said, adding that "it is in nobody's interest" to have these ships sailing around in the world's oceans.

She pointed out that these tankers undermine the maritime order and increase the risk of accidents and environmental damage.

"Every country should use its leverage with Russia to ask it not to use the fleet," she told DW, noting that ultimately all countries suffer the consequences.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

To clamp down on the fleet and curb Russia's oil export revenues, the United States and European countries have stepped up efforts to intercept tankers accused of violating sanctions.

The Trump administration, however, is reportedly considering lifting sanctions on some shadow fleet vessels and allowing them to transport oil that is not subject to sanctions.

A US official told Reuters earlier this month that the move was intended to ease record-high global freight rates.

Industry observers note that lifting sanctions on the shadow fleet "would decrease the effectiveness of the sanctions regime overall," remarked Michael Carpenter, senior fellow for Transatlantic Affairs at the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS). Such a move "rewards the aggressor and helps Moscow gain revenues to continue attacking Ukraine," he told DW.

"This is the exact opposite of what the US should be doing if it wants to end the war.".

Carpenter, who previously served as US ambassador to the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), said any sanctions relief would also put the US and the EU "strategically at odds with each other, with the EU clearly backing Ukraine and the US increasingly supporting Russia's financial goals.".

This view is shared by Ben Harris, vice president and director of Economic Studies at the Brookings Institution.

Lifting sanctions on shadow fleet tankers would "make it substantially easier for Russia to trade its oil at market rates," he noted, pointing out that it would "improve its government finances since so much revenue is tied to energy markets.".

US Energy Secretary Chris Wright, however, rejected suggestions that the US was removing sanctions from shadow fleet tankers.

According to recent reports, "We are converting dark tankers to legitimate tankers," Bloomberg quoted Wright as saying last week. "There is no removing of sanctions," he stressed, adding that the US government was working with investors who buy idle sanctioned tankers, refurbish them and use them to transport oil that is not subject to sanctions.

"We're going to move some of the ships from what I call the 'bad-guy fleet' to the 'good-guy fleet,'" Wright noted. "They will not carry sanctioned oil anymore.".

The US government has yet to unveil a detailed plan for shadow fleet tankers.

The proposal follows a deal that US President Donald Trump struck with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin this month to allow sales of Russian diesel onto global markets.

The agreement was seen as part of Trump's efforts to lower domestic fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3.

The US president also waived broad upcoming sanctions on Russia authorized by ​a recent legislation, which targeted Moscow's energy revenues and threatened tariffs against the world's largest purchasers of Russian oil and gas.

The decision was sharply criticized by Ukraine and its European allies over concerns that it could undermine the credibility of sanctions and weaken Western economic pressure on Moscow.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Harris remarked that "the US sanctions carry outsized weight because of the threat [for countries and businesses] of being cut off from the US financial system.".

If the US steps away from its sanctions on the shadow fleet, he argued, "the responsibility shifts to European policymakers." But they have "less effective options because of the diminished threat of severing financial ties.".

Still, the expert stressed that Europe has some tools, pointing to the continent's key role in global shipping and insurance services.

"They can implement measures demanding that tankers carry legitimate and established insurance when traveling through their waters," he said, noting that it "would mean that many shadow fleet tankers could not in practice legally transport Russian oil.".

Harris added that European policymakers could also pressure countries worldwide to better regulate the tankers flying their flags.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Carpenter remarked even if US eases some restrictions, the EU will have no choice but to continue enforcing its sanctions on these vessels.

"The vast majority of the shadow fleet traverses the Baltic Sea and exits it via the Danish Strait," he noted, adding that the EU is "uniquely positioned to board and inspect vessels moving through this key chokepoint.".

But Russia has threatened to seize ships belonging to European countries in retaliation for interdicting and seizing Russian vessels suspected of being part of the shadow fleet.

And without US backing, Carpenter mentioned, "it will be harder for EU countries to take on the burdens and risks of sanctions enforcement.".

Braw echoed this view, saying that Ukraine's European allies will have to remain united and continue working closely with partners such as Japan, Australia and Canada. Nevertheless, she stressed that what they can achieve on their own "is far less than what they can achieve if the US is part of the team.".

  • England will play Norway in the quarter-finals of the UEFA Nations League.
  • The Three Lions progressed to the last eight as League A Group 3 winners, having collected 15 points from six matches, including a sensational 3-2 win over Spain on the final matchday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Knapton | 20 Nov 2026 11:28, Last updated: 20 Nov 2026 11:47.

England will play Norway in the quarter-finals of the UEFA Nations League.

The Three Lions progressed to the last eight as League A Group 3 winners, having collected 15 points from six matches, including a sensational 3-2 win over Spain on the final matchday.

England's first-placed status meant that they entered the draw as one of the four seeded quarter-finalists, alongside France, Germany and Portugal, while they were unable to be drawn against Spain having already faced them in the group stage.

Thomas Tuchel's side will therefore do battle with Erling Haaland's Norway, who finished as runners-up to Portugal in League A Group 4 and will be seeking revenge for their World Cup 2026 quarter-final defeat to England.

Should England prevail in their reunion with the Scandinavians, they will clash with either Belgium or Germany in the semi-finals, for the right to contest a heavyweight showpiece event.

?????????? Thomas Tuchel's #ThreeLions will face Norway in the Nations League quarter-finals in March! https://t.co/TQBDCd9I4i.

The headline quarter-final sees reigning world and European champions Spain square off with France, a repeat of the 2020-21 Nations League final which Les Bleus won 2-1.

Whoever wins that clash of the titans will pit their wits against either the Netherlands or Portugal, who also squared off in the final of the inaugural Nations League in 2019; the Selecao triumphed 1-0 thanks to a Goncalo Guedes strike.

The first legs of the Nations League quarter-finals will take place between March 25 and March 27, before the return fixtures are held across March 28 and March 30.

England will travel to Norway for their first clash, before welcoming the Nordic nation to Wembley for the return fixture. The semi-finals and final will then be held in June in an as yet undetermined host nation.

Meanwhile, the Republic of Ireland will take on Croatia in the League A/League B playoffs for the right to earn promotion to the top tier, while Wales must beat Slovenia to retain their League A status.

Wales finished bottom of League A Group 4 on three points, but survived automatic relegation to the second division thanks to their superior points total to Turkey and the Czech Republic (both 0).

The Dragons have only ever faced Slovenia once before, drawing 0-0 in a 2005 international friendly.

Ireland's runners-up finish in League B Group 3 means that they have the chance to rise to League A for the first time ever, having only competed in League B since the Nations League's inception.

The Boys in Green have only beaten Croatia twice in their previous seven meetings, though, and lost 3-1 during their most recent head-to-head at Euro 2012.

Volkswagen logs Q3 operating loss of €5.86 billion on Porsche writedown

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Volkswagen Group on Thursday posted its worst quarterly numbers in more than a decade.
  • The company reported an operating loss of €5.86 billion (roughly $6.53 billion) during July, August and September.
  • The world's second-largest carmaker is battling mounting competition from and falling demand in the core Chinese market.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Volkswagen Group on Thursday posted its worst quarterly numbers in more than a decade.

The company reported an operating loss of €5.86 billion (roughly $6.53 billion) during July, August and September. One-off costs, not least a massive writedown in its stake in struggling sister company Porsche, explained the vast bulk of the losses.

The world's second-largest carmaker is battling mounting competition from and falling demand in the core Chinese market.

It is pursuing a major restructuring and downsizing program, trying to bolster falling profit margins, and executives stated the difficulties highlighted the urgency of this process.

In a recent development, "The nine-month results make one thing clear: We cannot afford to lose any time. We must act promptly and decisively," chief financial officer Arno Antlitz said in a video statement.

The results were the latest reminder of the pressure on VW — and the wider German and Western automotive industry — to react to increasing competition in China, high costs and practical difficulties moving towards electric car production, and unpredictable and rising tariff burdens, thanks in no small part to US President Donald Trump.

Here are some of the key Q3 figures:.

And here are some of the key year-to-date 9-month figures:.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

VW shares were already at their lowest levels in well over 10 years prior to Thursday's announcements, after months of difficult headlines and the ongoing aims to shed tens of thousands of jobs and reduce production capacities.

Perhaps as a result of this, the stock dipped briefly as markets opened and the news was published, but then started to rally as the day progressed.

By midday in Frankfurt, VW shares had climbed by 2% compared to their prices at the start of trading on the DAX.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

CEO Oliver Blume aims to shed around 100,000 jobs across the group, which includes the Audi and Porsche brands, in the coming years though a combination of layoffs and not replacing departing or retiring personnel.

Multiple factors are contributing to this. They include increased competition from Chinese manufacturers, falling revenues in China, changeable US auto tariffs under President Donald Trump, different staffing requirements when manufacturing electric cars and difficulties moving towards making and selling more electric cars at the pace once designated by political leaders.

Up to four plants in Germany could face closure as part of the plan, which has met with considerable union resistance and could lead to strikes starting next year.

CFO Antlitz said the figures demonstrated the urgency underlying these plans, saying the tech giant needed to increase its profit margins by 2030 to solidify its finances.

Antlitz said the operating return on sales was only 3.8% in the first nine months of the year, even before the one-off writedowns hitting the bottom line.

"That is not enough in the long term," he stated.

As part of its restructuring program, the VW Group aims to restore an operating profit margin of between 8-10% by 2030.

This year, amid one-off costs now totaling in the region of €10 billion, it expects a profit margin of no more than 1%, compared to prior forecasts in the region of 5%.
